meta.blurb: A teacher with a few students and one big idea: that anyone can become a better person. Confucius spoke simply about learning, family, honesty and kindness, and his students wrote it all down. Meet him through short sayings and small, human stories.
meta.bible:
The Analects: a book of 20 short books of sayings and conversations of Confucius and his students, collected by his followers after his death; the Chinese title Lunyu means Selected Sayings. Confucius: the teacher, also called Kongzi or Master Kong and called the Master by his students; he lived from about 551 BC to about 479 BC. Lu: the small state in China where he was born. Qi, Wei, Chen: other states where he travelled. Yan Hui: his favourite student, also called Yan Yuan, poor and joyful, who died young. Zilu: a brave, quick student, also called Ji Lu. Zigong: a clever, eloquent student. Zengzi: a thoughtful student. Ran Qiu: a student, sometimes called Ran You. Zai Wo: a student who slept in the day. Zhonggong: a student who asked about humaneness. You Ruo: a student. Gongxi Hua: a student who asked why. Ji Kangzi: a powerful minister of Lu. Duke Jing: the ruler of Qi. The Duke of Wei: the ruler of Wei. Yao and Shun: legendary sage-kings of ancient China. The gentleman: a person of good character; the word means the noble person; the small person is someone who thinks only of his own gain. Humaneness: goodness toward others, called ren in Chinese; it is the quality that Confucius valued most. Ritual: the courteous forms of good conduct, called li. The Way: the right path of living and ruling. Heaven: the higher power that Confucius spoke of with respect. Voice and tone: calm, clear, warm and respectful; each beat names the book of the Analects it comes from; everything is attributed to Confucius or his students and nothing is invented; there is no preaching. Additions for the full version: the book is told in the order of the twenty books of the Analects, ten beats to each, and Confucius is also called Qiu, his personal name, and Zhongni, his courtesy name. Duke Ai and Duke Ding: rulers of Lu in Confucius's later life. Zixia: a student, also called Bu Shang or Shang. Zizhang: a student, also called Shi. Ziyou: a student, also called Yan Yan or You. Fan Chi: a student, also called Fan Xu. Sima Niu: a student. Min Ziqian: a student known for his goodness to his parents. Ran Boniu: a student who fell ill. Tantai Mieming: a man of Wucheng praised by Ziyou. Zeng Dian: the father of Zengzi, a student who loved the spring. Yan Lu: the father of Yan Hui. Kong Li: the son of Confucius, also called Boyu. Chen Gang: a man who asked Boyu what his father taught him, also called Ziqin. Gongye Chang: a man whom Confucius gave his daughter in marriage. Kong Wenzi: an official of Wei. Zichan: a wise minister of Zheng. Yan Pingzhong: an official of Qi, a good friend to others. Ji Wenzi: an official of Lu who thought three times. Meng Zhifan: a modest soldier of Lu. Lin Fang: a man of Lu who asked about the root of ritual. Wangsun Jia: an official of Wei. Tai Bo: an early prince who gave up the throne. Yu: the Great Yu, a sage-king. Tang: the founder of the Shang dynasty, also called the Yin. Zhou: the dynasty after the Shang, begun by King Wen and King Wu; the Duke of Zhou was brother to King Wu. Meng Jingzi: a minister of Lu who visited Zengzi. Kuang: a town where Confucius was in danger. Huan Tui: a man of Song who threatened Confucius. Yang Huo: a powerful official of Lu. Liuxia Hui: a judge of Lu. Jieyu: the Madman of Chu, who sang to Confucius. Changju and Jieni: two ploughing farmers. Weizi, Jizi and Bi Gan: three humane men of the Yin dynasty. Ru Bei: a man who wished to see Confucius. Qu Boyu: a gentleman of Wei. Yuan Xian: a student. Nangong Kuo: a man of Lu. Master Mian: a blind music master. Odes: the old Book of Odes, about three hundred poems that Confucius loved and taught. Pole Star: the northern star, which seems to stay still while others turn. Yi River: a river in Lu. Zhuanyu: a small state. Chu: a large southern state.
 Mencius: a later Confucian writer. Bo Yi and Shu Qi: two brothers who would not serve a ruler they thought wrong. Shao Lian and Yu Zhong: other men who withdrew from public life. Gongsun Chao: an official who asked Zigong about Confucius. Yang Fu: a judge who asked Zengzi for advice. Ji Huanzi: a minister of the Ji family who accepted the singing girls. Chen Ziqin: also called Chen Gang. Duke of She: a ruler of the south who asked about uprightness. Weizi: a Yin man who left the cruel king. Wucheng: the town governed by Ziyou. Meng: one of the three great families of Lu. Qi: the large state next to Lu. Song: a state where Huan Tui lived. Zheng: the state of Zichan. Wei: the state of Duke Ling and Qu Boyu.

beats.scene: An old teacher sits under a tree speaking to a circle of students
beats.summary: Introduces Confucius, born about 551 BC in Lu, and the Analects, the book of his sayings collected by his followers.

beats.scene: A student reads a scroll by a window as a friend arrives
beats.summary: Book 1: the first two questions are about the pleasure of learning and the joy of a friend visiting.

beats.scene: A calm scholar in plain clothes smiles as people walk past without noticing him
beats.summary: Book 1: the third question, about not being resentful when others do not know you, and worrying more about knowing others.

beats.scene: Zengzi sits alone at night with a small lamp, thinking over his day
beats.summary: Book 1: Zengzi examines himself each day on three points.

beats.scene: A young man bows to his father at a family meal
beats.summary: Book 1: You Ruo says that respect at home is the root of humaneness.

beats.scene: A smooth-talking man charms a crowd while a plain man listens quietly
beats.summary: Book 1: Confucius says clever words and a pleasing face are seldom a sign of humaneness.

beats.scene: A young man bows to his elders at home, then studies by lamplight
beats.summary: Book 1: the young should be respectful at home, careful and trustworthy outside, loving to all, and should study with their spare energy.

beats.scene: A man tears up a flawed letter and calmly begins again
beats.summary: Book 1: a gentleman without seriousness earns no respect; when he makes a mistake he should not fear to change.

beats.scene: A poor man and a rich man listen to a teacher beside a river
beats.summary: Book 1: Zigong asks about being poor without flattery; Confucius says being poor and happy is better, and Zigong answers with a poem about polishing jade.

beats.scene: A ruler walks among farmers at harvest while officials count the grain
beats.summary: Book 1: to lead a state, be serious, keep your word, spend carefully, love the people, and call them to work only at the right time.

beats.scene: A single bright star shines over a quiet sleeping village
beats.summary: Book 2: a ruler who governs by good character is like the Pole Star.

beats.scene: A student reads a book of old poems while a bird sings outside
beats.summary: Book 2: Confucius says that the three hundred poems of the Odes can be summed up in one phrase, “no twisted thoughts”.

beats.scene: A kind ruler talks with villagers while a guard stands unused behind him
beats.summary: Book 2: rule by punishments makes people avoid wrongdoing without shame; rule by virtue makes them feel shame and correct themselves.

beats.scene: A white-haired man stands on a hill and looks back along a winding road
beats.summary: Book 2: Confucius sums up his own life in stages from fifteen to seventy.

beats.scene: An old woman is fed by her grown son at a plain table
beats.summary: Book 2: Ziyou asks about filial piety; Confucius says feeding parents is not enough, since dogs and horses are fed too, and respect is what matters.

beats.scene: A teacher opens an old scroll to show a student something new
beats.summary: Book 2: one who keeps old knowledge alive and so understands what is new is fit to be a teacher.

beats.scene: A student sits among scrolls and looks up at the sky, thinking
beats.summary: Book 2: learning without thinking is wasted, and thinking without learning is dangerous.

beats.scene: Confucius speaks to young Zilu, strong and impatient, in a courtyard
beats.summary: Book 2: Confucius teaches Zilu that knowing means admitting what you do not know.

beats.scene: A duke leans forward on his throne to ask a question of Confucius
beats.summary: Book 2: Duke Ai asks how to win the people; Confucius says to promote the upright over the crooked.

beats.scene: A man hesitates beside a fallen cart while others walk past
beats.summary: Book 2: to see what is right and not do it is a lack of courage.

beats.scene: A noble family dances in a great courtyard while an old teacher frowns
beats.summary: Book 3: the Ji family used eight rows of dancers in their courtyard, a right only for the king; Confucius asks what could not be tolerated if this can be.

beats.scene: A man in fine silk stands before a bronze bell with a hollow look
beats.summary: Book 3: a person without humaneness has no use for ritual or music.

beats.scene: Lin Fang questions Confucius in a quiet hall near a family altar
beats.summary: Book 3: Lin Fang asks what is the root of ritual; Confucius says better to be plain than lavish, and in mourning better to feel real grief than to show correct form.

beats.scene: A painter lays down a brush beside a clean white silk
beats.summary: Book 3: Zixia asks about a poem on a beautiful face; Confucius says the painting comes after the plain white ground; Zixia sees that ritual comes after, and Confucius praises him.

beats.scene: Confucius bows before an altar as if someone were truly there
beats.summary: Book 3: Confucius sacrificed to the ancestors as if they were present, and said that if he did not take part himself, it was as if he had not sacrificed.

beats.scene: A man kneels at a small kitchen stove while Confucius shakes his head
beats.summary: Book 3: Wangsun Jia asks whether it is better to flatter the stove than the corner of the house; Confucius says one who offends Heaven has nowhere to pray.

beats.scene: Confucius asks a temple keeper a question at every stone of the ancestral hall
beats.summary: Book 3: in the Grand Temple Confucius asked about everything; when mocked, he said that this was itself ritual.

beats.scene: Zigong holds a lamb by the rope while Confucius shakes his head gently
beats.summary: Book 3: Zigong wants to stop the sacrifice of a sheep at the new moon; Confucius says he loves the sheep but the Master loves the ritual.

beats.scene: A duke and his minister sit across from each other and bow
beats.summary: Book 3: Duke Ding asks how a ruler should employ ministers and how ministers should serve; Confucius says with ritual, and with loyalty.

beats.scene: A border guard bows to Confucius while students wait on the road
beats.summary: Book 3: an official at Yi says that Heaven will make Confucius a wooden bell clapper to wake the world.

beats.scene: A man chooses a house in a quiet village of kind neighbours
beats.summary: Book 4: it is beautiful to live among the humane; one who does not choose this is not wise.

beats.scene: A man carries home a bag of gold from a dark alley, looking uneasy
beats.summary: Book 4: everyone wants wealth and honour, but a gentleman will not keep them if gained wrongly, and does not leave humaneness for even a meal.

beats.scene: An old man sits at dawn on a hill and listens to the morning
beats.summary: Book 4: Confucius says that if you hear the Way in the morning, you may die in the evening without regret.

beats.scene: A scholar in a patched robe walks past a rich man's feast
beats.summary: Book 4: a scholar who aims at the Way but is ashamed of poor clothes and food is not worth talking with.

beats.scene: A merchant leans over a counter and presses a coin into a farmer's palm
beats.summary: Book 4: acting only for profit brings much resentment.

beats.scene: Two men at a market: one checks a fair weight, one counts coins
beats.summary: Book 4: the gentleman asks what is right; the small person asks what pays.

beats.scene: A young man watches a skilled craftsman at work and a sleeping idler
beats.summary: Book 4: when you see a worthy person, try to equal them; when you see an unworthy one, look at yourself.

beats.scene: An old man leans on a staff as his son stands beside him
beats.summary: Book 4: when parents are wrong, remonstrate gently; do not travel far while they live, and know their age with both gladness and fear.

beats.scene: A quiet man mends a neighbour's broken gate without a word
beats.summary: Book 4: the gentleman wants to be slow in speech and quick in action.

beats.scene: Neighbours share a lamp and a meal on a small village street
beats.summary: Book 4: virtue is never alone; it always has neighbours.

beats.scene: Confucius gives his daughter's hand to a young man freed from prison
beats.summary: Book 5: Gongye Chang had been in prison, but not for any crime, so Confucius gave him his daughter in marriage.

beats.scene: Zigong stands before Confucius beside a row of bronze ritual vessels
beats.summary: Book 5: Zigong asks what sort of person he is; Confucius says a vessel, and a precious sacrificial one.

beats.scene: A quiet student listens while another man talks quickly to a crowd
beats.summary: Book 5: someone says Zhonggong is humane but not eloquent; Confucius asks what use eloquence is, since a ready tongue makes people dislike you.

beats.scene: A student sleeps at his desk in the afternoon while the teacher watches
beats.summary: Book 5: Zai Wo sleeps by day; Confucius is sharp with him and says he now watches deeds as well as words.

beats.scene: A senior official asks a young clerk a question about a hard point
beats.summary: Book 5: Zigong asks why Kong Wenzi was called 'Wen', cultured; Confucius says he was quick, loved learning and was not ashamed to ask those below him.

beats.scene: A minister of Zheng walks with an escort through a crowded market
beats.summary: Book 5: Confucius says the minister Zichan followed four ways of the gentleman: modest in conduct, respectful to superiors, kind to the people, and just in using them.

beats.scene: Two old friends of many years share tea and bow to each other
beats.summary: Book 5: Yan Pingzhong was good at friendship; even after a long acquaintance he treated friends with respect.

beats.scene: An official sits alone at his desk, thinking before he acts
beats.summary: Book 5: Ji Wenzi thought three times before acting; Confucius says twice is enough.

beats.scene: Three men sit together by a fire, each telling his wish
beats.summary: Book 5: Zilu, Yan Yuan and Confucius each say what they most wish for.

beats.scene: A small village of ten houses at dusk with one lamp in a window
beats.summary: Book 5: in a village of ten households there must be someone as loyal and trustworthy as Confucius, but not as fond of learning.

beats.scene: Duke Ai leans forward as Confucius speaks of a student who died young
beats.summary: Book 6: Duke Ai asks which student loved learning; Confucius names Yan Hui, who never vented his anger on others or repeated a mistake, but whose life was short.

beats.scene: A steward counts grain into a sack at a quiet village house
beats.summary: Book 6: Ran Qiu asks grain for the mother of Gongxi Hua, who is away on a mission; he gives far more than Confucius suggested, and Confucius says a gentleman helps the needy, not the rich.

beats.scene: A young man looks out over a river while messengers wait at his door
beats.summary: Book 6: the Ji family wants Min Ziqian as steward of a town; he asks the messenger to decline politely, or he will be across the Wen River.

beats.scene: A thin young man happily eats rice from a bowl in a narrow lane
beats.summary: Book 6: Yan Hui lives on little in a narrow lane and never loses his joy.

beats.scene: A town magistrate talks with a young man who walks only the main road
beats.summary: Book 6: Ziyou, magistrate of Wucheng, is asked if he has found good men; he names Tantai Mieming, who never takes shortcuts and visits only on public business.

beats.scene: A soldier rides last behind a retreating army, whipping his horse at the gate
beats.summary: Book 6: Meng Zhifan, retreating after a defeat, stayed at the rear and said at the gate that his horse would not go forward.

beats.scene: A rough farmer and a pale clerk stand on either side of a gentleman
beats.summary: Book 6: where plain nature outweighs polish a man is rustic; where polish outweighs nature he is a scribe; only when balanced is he a gentleman.

beats.scene: A student studies with a bright smile in a warm lamp-lit room
beats.summary: Book 6: knowing is good, loving is better, and delighting is best.

beats.scene: One man gazes at a bright stream, another sits calm before a mountain
beats.summary: Book 6: the wise delight in water, the humane in mountains; the wise are active, the humane calm; the wise are joyful, the humane long-lived.

beats.scene: Two travellers help each other climb a steep hill together
beats.summary: Book 6: Zigong asks about helping everyone; Confucius says the humane person helps others to succeed.

beats.scene: Confucius sits among old scrolls and tells his students about the ancient sages
beats.summary: Book 7: Confucius says he passes on old wisdom and does not invent new ideas.

beats.scene: Confucius sits alone at dusk with a lamp, thinking about his faults
beats.summary: Book 7: Confucius says his worries are not cultivating virtue, not explaining what he has learned, not moving toward what is right, and not changing what is not good.

beats.scene: A traveller walks a road at sunrise carrying a lute and a bow
beats.summary: Book 7: set your heart on the Way, hold to virtue, rely on humaneness, and wander in the arts.

beats.scene: A teacher shows a student one corner of a square wooden board
beats.summary: Book 7: Confucius teaches only those who are eager; if shown one corner, they should find the other three.

beats.scene: Zilu faces Confucius beside a river and asks about leading an army
beats.summary: Book 7: Zilu asks whom Confucius would take to lead armies; not the reckless, but one who is careful and plans well.

beats.scene: A man sleeps happily with his arm as a pillow beside a simple meal
beats.summary: Book 7: joy can be found in plain food and water; wealth gained wrongly is like a floating cloud.

beats.scene: Confucius walks along a road with two companions at sunset
beats.summary: Book 7: whenever three people walk together, Confucius finds a teacher among them.

beats.scene: Confucius and his students rest under a tree as armed men approach
beats.summary: Book 7: when Huan Tui threatened him, Confucius said that Heaven had given him his virtue, so what could Huan Tui do to him?

beats.scene: Confucius fishes with a single line at a quiet bend of the river
beats.summary: Book 7: Confucius fished with a line, not a net, and shot at flying birds, not at roosting ones.

beats.scene: Confucius greets his students, standing straight with a warm and calm face
beats.summary: Book 7: the students describe their teacher as gentle but stern, dignified but not harsh, respectful and at ease.

beats.scene: A prince quietly leaves a palace by a narrow path at dawn
beats.summary: Book 8: Tai Bo gave up the right to rule three times, so quietly that the people could find no words to praise him.

beats.scene: A courtier bows stiffly in a hall while a rude man shouts nearby
beats.summary: Book 8: without ritual, respect becomes tiring, caution becomes timidity, courage becomes disorder, and frankness becomes rudeness.

beats.scene: A dying old man shows his hands to a circle of students
beats.summary: Book 8: Zengzi, dying, asks his students to look at his hands and feet; he quotes the Odes about walking on thin ice and says he is now free of harm.

beats.scene: A minister sits beside a sick man's bed while a lamp burns low
beats.summary: Book 8: Zengzi, ill, tells Meng Jingzi that a dying bird's cry is sad but a dying man's words are good, and names three things the gentleman values in the Way.

beats.scene: A scholar bows to a younger man in a courtyard and asks a question
beats.summary: Book 8: Zengzi remembers a friend who, though able, asked those who were not, who had much but seemed to have little, and who did not strike back when offended.

beats.scene: Zengzi walks a long road with a heavy load on his back
beats.summary: Book 8: Zengzi says a scholar's burden is heavy and his road is long, and it ends only with death.

beats.scene: A student recites poems, bows at a shrine and plays a small drum
beats.summary: Book 8: a person is stirred by the Odes, made firm by ritual and completed by music.

beats.scene: A student races up a steep stair of books, afraid of falling behind
beats.summary: Book 8: learn as if you could never catch up, and as if you were afraid of losing what you have.

beats.scene: A great ruler gazes up at the open sky with his hands behind him
beats.summary: Book 8: Confucius praises Yao: only Heaven is great, and only Yao took Heaven as his model; the people could find no words for his goodness.

beats.scene: A king in a plain robe digs a canal beside a low house
beats.summary: Book 8: Confucius finds no fault in Yu, who ate plain food but honoured the spirits, dressed poorly but wore fine ritual robes, and lived in a low house but put his strength into canals.

beats.scene: Confucius stands calmly while his students argue loudly behind him
beats.summary: Book 9: Confucius was free of four faults: guessing, insisting on certainty, obstinacy and putting himself first.

beats.scene: Armed men surround Confucius and his students in a small walled town
beats.summary: Book 9: surrounded in Kuang, Confucius says that Heaven gave him the culture of King Wen, so the men of Kuang can do nothing to him.

beats.scene: A grand minister questions Zigong about the Master's many skills
beats.summary: Book 9: a minister asks whether Confucius is a sage since he has so many skills; Confucius says he was poor in youth and so learned many humble skills.

beats.scene: A simple farmer asks a question while Confucius thinks hard
beats.summary: Book 9: Confucius says he has no special knowledge; when a simple man asked him something and his mind was blank, he tapped at both ends of the question until he had answered it.

beats.scene: Yan Yuan gazes up at a towering mountain peak with a sigh
beats.summary: Book 9: Yan Yuan sighs that the Master's way rises higher the more he looks up, leads him step by step, and when he wishes to follow he finds no road.

beats.scene: Zigong holds out a gleaming jade disc in a wooden case
beats.summary: Book 9: Zigong asks whether a beautiful jade should be hidden in a box or sold; Confucius says sell it, and that he is waiting for the right price.

beats.scene: Confucius stands on a riverbank watching the water flow past
beats.summary: Book 9: standing by a river, Confucius says everything passes like this, day and night.

beats.scene: A man pours the last basket of earth onto a nearly finished mound
beats.summary: Book 9: like piling up a mountain, stopping one basket short is one's own doing; like levelling ground, even one basket added is progress.

beats.scene: A frosty hillside where pine and cypress stand green among bare trees
beats.summary: Book 9: only when the year grows cold do we see that the pine and cypress are the last to lose their leaves.

beats.scene: A lone man stands calmly as a great army marches past
beats.summary: Book 9: an army can lose its commander, but no one can take away the will of an ordinary person.

beats.scene: Confucius speaks quietly with villagers, then clearly in the ancestral temple
beats.summary: Book 10: in his home village Confucius was modest and seemed hardly able to speak, but in the temple and at court he spoke clearly and carefully.

beats.scene: Confucius chats with junior officials, then bows to senior ones at court
beats.summary: Book 10: at court Confucius spoke affably with junior officials, frankly but respectfully with senior ones, and with reverence and ease before the ruler.

beats.scene: Confucius bows his head under a high gate as if it were too low
beats.summary: Book 10: entering the duke's gate, Confucius bent his body as if the gate were too small to admit him, and did not step on the threshold.

beats.scene: Confucius eats a modest meal quietly with a slice of ginger beside the bowl
beats.summary: Book 10: Confucius would not eat spoiled or out-of-season food, kept to modest portions, always took a little ginger, and did not talk while eating.

beats.scene: Confucius sets aside a few grains of rice before eating a simple meal
beats.summary: Book 10: even with coarse rice and vegetable soup, Confucius made a small offering before eating, always with reverence.

beats.scene: A calm official returns from court to a burned stable in the morning
beats.summary: Book 10: when his stable burned, Confucius asked only whether anyone was hurt.

beats.scene: Confucius arranges a funeral for a friend who has no family
beats.summary: Book 10: when a friend died with no one to take charge, Confucius said he would see to the burial; for a gift of carriage and horses he did not bow, unless it was sacrificial meat.

beats.scene: Confucius sets off on foot at once while his carriage is still being prepared
beats.summary: Book 10: when the ruler summoned him, Confucius set off on foot without waiting for the horses to be yoked.

beats.scene: Confucius bows politely toward a blind musician led across a hall
beats.summary: Book 10: Confucius showed courtesy to people in mourning, to officials in formal dress and to the blind, even when he knew them well.

beats.scene: Confucius stands upright in a carriage, holding the strap, looking straight ahead
beats.summary: Book 10: in a carriage Confucius stood straight and held the strap, and did not look around, speak in haste or point.

beats.scene: Four groups of students sit together, some with scrolls and some with spears
beats.summary: Book 11: Confucius remembers the students who stayed with him in hard times and names those outstanding in virtue, speech, government and learning.

beats.scene: Two students argue while Zigong asks the teacher who is better
beats.summary: Book 11: Zigong asks whether Zizhang or Zixia is better; Confucius says one goes too far and the other not far enough, and too far is as bad as not enough.

beats.scene: A young man plays a zither beside a gate while students whisper
beats.summary: Book 11: students look down on Zilu's zither playing; Confucius says Zilu has ascended the hall but not yet entered the inner rooms.

beats.scene: Two students ask the same question and the teacher answers differently
beats.summary: Book 11: Zilu and Ran Qiu ask whether to act at once; Confucius answers each differently, and explains why.

beats.scene: Yan Yuan hurries along a dusty road after the others
beats.summary: Book 11: after danger in Kuang, Yan Yuan arrived late; Confucius said he thought him dead, and Yan Yuan said that while the Master lived he would not dare to die.

beats.scene: A grieving old teacher bows his head beside an empty seat
beats.summary: Book 11: Yan Hui dies, and Confucius weeps bitterly, asking for whom he should grieve if not for him.

beats.scene: An old father asks Confucius for his carriage while a coffin waits
beats.summary: Book 11: Yan Lu asks for Confucius's carriage to make an outer coffin for Yan Hui; Confucius refuses, saying his own son had none and he could not go on foot.

beats.scene: Students carry a lavish coffin while Confucius turns away in sorrow
beats.summary: Book 11: the students bury Yan Hui lavishly against Confucius's wish; he says Hui treated him as a father but he could not treat Hui as a son.

beats.scene: Zilu bows before Confucius beside a quiet family shrine
beats.summary: Book 11: Zilu asks about serving the spirits and about death; Confucius turns him back to serving people and understanding life.

beats.scene: A young man sets down his zither and speaks of bathing in spring
beats.summary: Book 11: Confucius asks four students their wishes; three speak of governing, but Zeng Dian wants to bathe in the Yi River in spring and walk home singing; Confucius sighs that he is with Dian.

beats.scene: A young student bows his head as the teacher speaks of humaneness
beats.summary: Book 12: Yan Yuan asks what humaneness is, and Confucius says it begins with mastering oneself.

beats.scene: A man opens his door to a guest with a deep, polite bow
beats.summary: Book 12: Confucius tells Zhonggong to treat everyone like an honoured guest and not to impose on others what he does not want himself.

beats.scene: A calm man walks home alone through a dark lane, unafraid
beats.summary: Book 12: Sima Niu asks about the gentleman; Confucius says he is free of worry and fear, because on looking inward he finds nothing wrong.

beats.scene: A man sits alone at a window while a friend speaks kindly to him
beats.summary: Book 12: Sima Niu laments having no brothers; Zixia says life and death are fated, and that a respectful gentleman has brothers everywhere within the four seas.

beats.scene: Stores of grain, a rack of weapons and a crowd of trusting villagers
beats.summary: Book 12: Zigong asks what a government needs; Confucius names food, weapons and trust, and says trust is the last to give up.

beats.scene: A duke looks at empty granaries while farmers bring in a poor harvest
beats.summary: Book 12: in a year of famine Duke Ai says he lacks revenue; You Ruo says to tax a tenth, since when the people have enough the ruler cannot be in want.

beats.scene: Duke Jing sits on his throne as a father and son stand before him
beats.summary: Book 12: Duke Jing asks about government; Confucius says each person must truly be what he is: ruler, minister, father, son.

beats.scene: A minister frowns at a locked storehouse while a thief watches from the dark
beats.summary: Book 12: Ji Kangzi worried about thieves; Confucius said that if he himself were not greedy, they would not steal even if rewarded.

beats.scene: Wind bends a field of tall grass as a minister looks on
beats.summary: Book 12: Ji Kangzi asks about punishing the wicked; Confucius says the ruler's character is the wind and the people are the grass.

beats.scene: Fan Chi listens as Confucius speaks of people and of love
beats.summary: Book 12: Fan Chi asks about humaneness and Confucius says to love people; about wisdom, and he says to know people.

beats.scene: Zilu scratches his head in surprise as Confucius explains calmly
beats.summary: Book 13: Confucius says that his first task in governing would be to put names right.

beats.scene: Fan Chi holds a hoe and asks the teacher about farming in a field
beats.summary: Book 13: Fan Chi asks about farming and gardening; Confucius says an old farmer knows better, and afterwards says a ruler who loves ritual, justice and trust will have people come to him from every side.

beats.scene: A scholar stands tongue-tied before a foreign court holding a roll of poems
beats.summary: Book 13: a man who can recite three hundred poems but cannot govern or answer for himself abroad has learned much but gained little.

beats.scene: A ruler sets a good example and workers follow without being told
beats.summary: Book 13: if the ruler is upright, things go well without orders; if he is not, they are not obeyed even when he commands.

beats.scene: A cart rolls through a crowded town with people on every street
beats.summary: Book 13: on seeing many people in Wei, Confucius says first make them prosperous, then teach them.

beats.scene: A teacher speaks to a ruler's envoy while workers build a bridge behind
beats.summary: Book 13: Confucius says that if a ruler would use him for one year, he could put things on a better course, and in three years the work would be done.

beats.scene: A father and a son stand before a magistrate while a village elder frowns
beats.summary: Book 13: the Duke of She says an upright man of his village testified against his father for stealing a sheep; Confucius says that in his village fathers shield sons and sons shield fathers, and uprightness lies in that.

beats.scene: Several musicians play different instruments that blend into one song
beats.summary: Book 13: the gentleman seeks harmony without sameness; the small person seeks sameness without harmony.

beats.scene: Zigong asks about a man whom every villager loves while Confucius thinks
beats.summary: Book 13: Zigong asks whether a man whom everyone in the village likes is good; Confucius says not enough, and that it is better if the good like him and the bad dislike him.

beats.scene: A calm man stands at ease beside a proud man who frowns
beats.summary: Book 13: the gentleman is at ease without being proud; the small person is proud without being at ease.

beats.scene: A student in a plain robe asks the teacher about shame
beats.summary: Book 14: Yuan Xian asks about shame; Confucius says it is shameful to think only of one's salary, whether the state is well governed or not.

beats.scene: A great archer and a strongman lie dead while a farmer plants a field
beats.summary: Book 14: Nangong Kuo says that the archer Yi and the strong Ao died violently while Yu and Ji, who farmed, won the world; Confucius is silent, then calls him a gentleman who values virtue.

beats.scene: A poor man works without complaint while a rich man gives proudly
beats.summary: Book 14: it is hard to be poor without resentment and easy to be rich without arrogance.

beats.scene: A student studies alone by lamplight while others show off to a crowd
beats.summary: Book 14: in ancient times people learned to improve themselves; now they learn to impress others.

beats.scene: A messenger sits respectfully beside Confucius, who pours him a cup of tea
beats.summary: Book 14: Qu Boyu's messenger says his master wants to make his faults fewer but has not managed it, and Confucius admires the answer.

beats.scene: Confucius smiles as Zigong says that he is describing himself
beats.summary: Book 14: Confucius says the humane are free of worry, the wise of doubt and the brave of fear, and claims to have mastered none; Zigong says the Master is describing himself.

beats.scene: A man holds up a set of scales while two neighbours talk
beats.summary: Book 14: asked about repaying harm with kindness, Confucius says to repay harm with fairness and kindness with kindness.

beats.scene: Confucius sits sighing at dusk while Zigong asks him a question
beats.summary: Book 14: Confucius says no one understands him; he blames neither Heaven nor people, studies what is near and reaches what is high, and only Heaven knows him.

beats.scene: A gate guard at a stone gate questions Zilu as night falls
beats.summary: Book 14: a gatekeeper asks where Zilu is from; hearing 'from Confucius', he calls him the man who knows it is no use yet goes on trying.

beats.scene: A man carrying a basket passes as Confucius strikes a stone chime
beats.summary: Book 14: a man with a basket hears Confucius playing the stone chime in Wei, says the player has a heart, then that he is stubborn and should give up; Confucius says only that the man is resolute.

beats.scene: Weary followers sit on a roadside while Confucius stays calm among them
beats.summary: Book 15: stranded without food in Chen, Confucius tells angry Zilu that the gentleman holds firm in hardship.

beats.scene: Zizhang writes a saying on his sash while Confucius watches
beats.summary: Book 15: Zizhang asks how to get on in the world; Confucius says to be loyal and trustworthy in speech and serious in action, and Zizhang writes it on his sash.

beats.scene: A man declines to speak with a stubborn listener who has turned away
beats.summary: Book 15: to fail to speak to someone who can be spoken with is to lose a person; to speak to someone who cannot be is to waste words; the wise lose neither.

beats.scene: A craftsman sharpens his chisel before carving a block of wood
beats.summary: Book 15: a craftsman must first sharpen his tools; one who ignores the distant future will have trouble near at hand.

beats.scene: A man at a table gently takes the blame while others quarrel
beats.summary: Book 15: be strict in judging yourself and lenient in judging others, and you will keep resentment far away.

beats.scene: A student reads by lamplight while a long road stretches ahead
beats.summary: Book 15: it is people who can make the Way great, not the Way that makes people great.

beats.scene: A man studies a crooked row of seedlings and begins to replant it
beats.summary: Book 15: to have a fault and not correct it is to have a fault indeed.

beats.scene: A student gently disagrees with his teacher, who nods approval
beats.summary: Book 15: when it comes to humaneness, do not yield even to your teacher.

beats.scene: Rich and poor students sit together in an open courtyard
beats.summary: Book 15: in teaching there are no classes.

beats.scene: Confucius leads a blind music master by the arm into a room
beats.summary: Book 15: Confucius guides the blind Music Master Mian to the steps and the mat and tells him who is present, saying that this is how to assist a music master.

beats.scene: A minister's army marches toward a small state while Confucius warns his students
beats.summary: Book 16: the Ji family plans to attack Zhuanyu; Confucius tells Ran Qiu and Zilu that a ruler should worry about unequal sharing, and that the Ji's trouble lies within his own court.

beats.scene: Three friends walk together: one upright, one honest, one carrying books
beats.summary: Book 16: Confucius names three kinds of helpful friends and three kinds of harmful friends.

beats.scene: Three friends laugh together at a table where music and books lie
beats.summary: Book 16: three enjoyments help (ritual and music, speaking of others' good, many worthy friends); three harm (extravagance, idle wandering, feasting).

beats.scene: A young man stands before an elder, waiting for the right moment to speak
beats.summary: Book 16: in attending a gentleman there are three errors: speaking before being asked, not speaking when asked, and speaking without watching his face.

beats.scene: Three men of different ages walk together: a youth, a grown man, an elder
beats.summary: Book 16: a gentleman guards against three things: in youth, lust; in his prime, quarrelsomeness; in old age, greed.

beats.scene: A gentleman bows toward the sky, an elder, and an old book
beats.summary: Book 16: the gentleman holds three things in awe: the will of Heaven, great people, and the words of the sages; the small person does not know the will of Heaven and does not fear it.

beats.scene: Four students sit at different desks: one reads easily, others struggle, one sleeps
beats.summary: Book 16: those born knowing are best; those who learn by study next; those who learn after meeting difficulty next; those who meet difficulty and do not learn are the lowest.

beats.scene: A gentleman looks at a far hill, hears a bird, and pauses before speaking
beats.summary: Book 16: the gentleman has nine things to think about: seeing clearly, hearing sharply, a warm face, a respectful manner, loyal speech, serious work, asking in doubt, the consequences of anger, and righteousness at the sight of gain.

beats.scene: A man leans away from a pot of boiling water, another reaches upward
beats.summary: Book 16: seeing the good, pursue it as if you could not catch up; seeing evil, pull back as if testing hot water.

beats.scene: A son hurries across a courtyard as his father calls to him
beats.summary: Book 16: Chen Gang asks Boyu whether his father taught him anything special; Boyu says only to study the Odes and the rites; Chen Gang learns three things, including that a gentleman keeps his distance from his son.

beats.scene: Two men meet by chance on a dusty road, one in a rich robe
beats.summary: Book 17: Yang Huo wants Confucius to serve him; they meet on the road, where Yang Huo says the years do not wait, and Confucius replies that he will take office.

beats.scene: Two seeds from one bag grow into very different plants
beats.summary: Book 17: by nature people are close to one another, but by practice they grow far apart.

beats.scene: A teacher smiles at the sound of strings and singing in a small town
beats.summary: Book 17: in Wucheng Confucius hears strings and singing and jokes about using an ox cleaver to kill a chicken; Ziyou reminds him of his own teaching, and Confucius admits he was joking.

beats.scene: Zizhang takes notes while the teacher counts five fingers
beats.summary: Book 17: Zizhang asks about humaneness; Confucius says it is to practise five things: respect, generosity, trustworthiness, diligence and kindness.

beats.scene: A student is lost in a maze of six paths
beats.summary: Book 17: Confucius tells Zilu of six virtues and six blindnesses: love of humaneness, knowledge, trust, straightness, courage and firmness, without love of learning, lead to foolishness, aimlessness, harm, rudeness, disorder and recklessness.

beats.scene: Students listen as the teacher reads poems aloud beside a pond with birds
beats.summary: Book 17: Confucius asks why none of his students study the Odes, which can stir the mind, sharpen observation, bring people together, give voice to complaint, and teach duty and the names of birds, beasts and plants.

beats.scene: Gifts of jade and silk lie beside a silent set of bells and drums
beats.summary: Book 17: Confucius asks whether ritual means only jade and silk, and whether music means only bells and drums.

beats.scene: A teacher sits silent beneath a wide sky while seasons change over fields
beats.summary: Book 17: Confucius says he would rather not speak; Zigong asks what the students could then pass on; Confucius says that Heaven does not speak, yet the four seasons turn and all things grow.

beats.scene: Confucius picks up a zither and sings inside while a visitor's messenger leaves
beats.summary: Book 17: Ru Bei wishes to see Confucius, who declines by saying he is ill; as the messenger leaves, Confucius takes up his zither and sings so that the man can hear.

beats.scene: Zai Wo stands before Confucius in fine silk beside a plain mourning robe
beats.summary: Book 17: Zai Wo says three years of mourning is too long; Confucius asks whether he would be at ease in fine food and brocade, tells him to do as he pleases, and later says that a child is held in its parents' arms for three years.

beats.scene: Three men on three roads: one leaves, one is chained, one faces a king
beats.summary: Book 18: three humane men of the Yin dynasty: Weizi left the cruel king, Jizi became his slave, and Bi Gan spoke out and was put to death.

beats.scene: A judge is led out of court, dismissed again, with a calm face
beats.summary: Book 18: Liuxia Hui, dismissed as judge three times, is asked why he does not leave; he says that serving people honestly means being dismissed anywhere.

beats.scene: Duke Jing of Qi speaks with advisers while Confucius waits outside
beats.summary: Book 18: Duke Jing of Qi says he will honour Confucius between the Ji and the Meng families; later he says he is too old to use him, and Confucius leaves.

beats.scene: Dancing girls arrive at a minister's palace as Confucius turns to leave
beats.summary: Book 18: the people of Qi sent singing girls to Lu; Ji Huanzi accepted them and for three days held no court; Confucius left.

beats.scene: A wild-haired man walks past Confucius's carriage, singing
beats.summary: Book 18: the Madman of Chu, Jieyu, passes Confucius singing of the phoenix: the past cannot be mended, the future can be pursued; Confucius gets down to speak with him, but he hurries away.

beats.scene: Two farmers plough a muddy field as a carriage waits at the river
beats.summary: Book 18: two farmers tell Zilu the world cannot be changed; Confucius says he must stay among people.

beats.scene: An old man with a basket weeds a field while Zilu waits
beats.summary: Book 18: Zilu, left behind on a journey, meets an old man with a basket and asks about his master; the old man says a person who does no labour is no master, then plants his staff and weeds, and Zilu waits respectfully.

beats.scene: A farmer serves chicken and millet to a traveller in a simple farmhouse
beats.summary: Book 18: the old man takes Zilu home, serves chicken and millet and introduces his sons; Confucius calls him a hermit, but he is gone when Zilu returns; Zilu says that to refuse to serve is wrong, even though they know the Way will not prevail.

beats.scene: Confucius stands among a row of seated hermits, each with his back turned
beats.summary: Book 18: Confucius reviews men who withdrew from the world, such as Bo Yi, Shu Qi and Liuxia Hui, and says he is different, having no fixed 'may' and 'may not'.

beats.scene: An old duke gives his son advice beside a row of ancestors' portraits
beats.summary: Book 18: the Duke of Zhou tells the Duke of Lu that a gentleman does not neglect his kin, does not make ministers resent being unused, does not abandon old friends without grave cause, and does not demand perfection from one person.

beats.scene: A student stands at the edge of a river, weighing a hard choice
beats.summary: Book 19: the sayings of the students after the Master's death begin with Zizhang: a scholar who sees danger gives his life, who sees gain thinks of right, who sacrifices thinks of reverence and who mourns thinks of grief.

beats.scene: Two students argue politely about whom they should accept as friends
beats.summary: Book 19: Zixia's students ask Zizhang about friendship; Zixia says to befriend the good and reject the rest, but Zizhang says a gentleman honours the worthy and tolerates everyone.

beats.scene: A student marks a calendar and rereads his notes by lamplight
beats.summary: Book 19: Zixia says that one who knows each day what he lacks and each month does not forget what he has learned can be called a lover of learning.

beats.scene: Craftsmen work in a workshop while a scholar studies in a library
beats.summary: Book 19: Zixia says that craftsmen dwell in workshops to accomplish their tasks, and gentlemen study to reach the Way.

beats.scene: A gentleman looks stern from afar, smiles up close, and speaks exactly
beats.summary: Book 19: Zixia says the gentleman shows three changes: from afar he looks stern, close up he is warm, and his words are exact.

beats.scene: A young judge bows to Zengzi before taking up his post
beats.summary: Book 19: Yang Fu, newly made a judge, asks Zengzi's advice; Zengzi says the rulers have lost the Way and the people are scattered, so he should feel pity, not joy, at uncovering a crime.

beats.scene: A crowd looks up at a dark eclipse, then at the shining sun again
beats.summary: Book 19: Zigong says a gentleman's faults are like eclipses of the sun and moon; everyone sees them, and when he mends them, everyone looks up to him.

beats.scene: An official asks Zigong where Confucius learned, as students listen
beats.summary: Book 19: Gongsun Chao asks Zigong who taught Confucius; Zigong says the Way of Kings Wen and Wu lives in people, and the Master learned from everyone.

beats.scene: A student points to a high wall with shining towers rising behind it
beats.summary: Book 19: Zigong says his own wall is shoulder-high but Confucius is like the sun and moon, which cannot be climbed.

beats.scene: Zigong stands before a tall mountain, speaking to Chen Ziqin
beats.summary: Book 19: Chen Ziqin says Zigong is only being modest; Zigong says that one word can show wisdom or folly, that the Master can no more be matched than Heaven can be climbed by stairs, and that in life he was glorious and in death mourned.

beats.scene: An aged king hands a staff to a younger man on a hill
beats.summary: Book 20: Yao tells Shun that the destiny of Heaven rests on him, to hold to the Mean sincerely, and that if the people suffer hardship, Heaven's gifts will end for ever; Shun gave the same charge to Yu.

beats.scene: A king in plain robes kneels before a black bull at an altar
beats.summary: Book 20: Tang, founder of the Shang dynasty, prays with a black bull that he will not pardon the guilty or hide the good, and that the blame for the people's faults should fall on him.

beats.scene: A king stands among surveyors with scales, measures and a map
beats.summary: Book 20: the early Zhou rulers gave generously, held that the people's faults should rest on them alone, set weights and measures in order, restored fallen states and raised hidden talents, and the people turned to them.

beats.scene: People bring grain to a market while a mourning family bows at a shrine
beats.summary: Book 20: what matters most is the people, food, mourning and sacrifice; generosity wins the multitude, trust brings trust, diligence achieves, and fairness brings gladness.

beats.scene: Zizhang kneels with a brush, writing down the teacher's two lists
beats.summary: Book 20: Zizhang asks how to govern; Confucius says to honour five excellences and banish four evils: generosity without waste, labour without resentment, desire without greed, dignity without pride, awe without harshness.

beats.scene: A ruler points to a hillside of fruit trees and a farmer nods
beats.summary: Book 20: generous without waste means benefiting people through what they already have; labour without resentment means choosing tasks they can do; desire without greed because the desire is for humaneness.

beats.scene: A gentleman in a neat cap and robe looks calmly ahead as people watch
beats.summary: Book 20: the gentleman, with many or few, never dares to be careless, so he is dignified without pride; he dresses properly and looks steadily, so that people look on him with awe but without fear.

beats.scene: A harsh official reads out a sentence while farmers stand nervously
beats.summary: Book 20: the four evils are killing without having taught, demanding results without warning, giving slack orders and then demanding speed, and being stingy in giving out what is due.

beats.scene: A man sits alone beside a simple grave under tall trees
beats.summary: Confucius died about 479 BC; his students mourned three years; according to Mencius, Zigong stayed on alone for three more.

beats.scene: Students of many lands read an open scroll together by lamplight
beats.summary: Book 20: the book ends with three kinds of understanding: destiny, ritual and words; readers still return to it today.

A1A2: Confucius was a great teacher in ancient China long ago.
Learning something new and using it brings real joy.
A good person is not angry when nobody knows him.
Every day Zengzi asked himself three questions about how he lived.
Love and respect at home are the roots of goodness.
Fine words and a smiling face do not always mean a good heart.
Young people should respect their family, be honest with others, and then study.
When you make a mistake, do not be afraid to change.
Confucius said it is even better to be poor and still happy.
A good leader keeps his word and does not waste money.
A good ruler is like a star that others follow.
Confucius loved the old poems, and he said they had honest thoughts.
Kind leaders teach people to be good, not afraid.
At seventy, Confucius could follow his heart without doing wrong.
Feeding your parents is not enough; you must also show respect.
If you study old things well, you can understand new things too.
Learning without thinking is a waste of time.
To know what you do not know is also knowledge.
Duke Ai asked how to win the hearts of his people.
If you know what is right, you must do it.
A rich family used a dance that only the king should use.
Without a good heart, nice manners and music mean nothing.
Confucius said real feeling matters more than a grand show.
Zixia learned that good manners grow from a good heart.
Confucius made offerings to the spirits as if they were really there.
Confucius said you cannot hide from Heaven when you do wrong.
In the temple Confucius asked about everything, even things he knew.
Zigong wanted to save a sheep, but Confucius loved the old ceremony.
A ruler should treat his helpers with respect, and they should be loyal.
A border guard said Heaven would use Confucius to teach the world.
It is good to live among kind people, and wise people choose it.
Everyone wants money, but a good person will not take it unfairly.
If you learn the Way in the morning, you can die happy at night.
A scholar should not be ashamed of old clothes and plain food.
Someone who thinks only about money makes many people unhappy.
A good person asks what is right, not what pays.
When you see a good person, try to be like them.
Be gentle when your parents are wrong, and do not go far from them.
A good person speaks slowly but acts quickly.
A good person will always find good neighbours.
Confucius believed Gongye Chang was innocent and let him marry his daughter.
Confucius told Zigong that he was like a fine and precious bowl.
Confucius said a quick tongue does not make a person good.
A student slept in the day, and Confucius was upset.
A wise person is not ashamed to ask those below him for help.
Confucius said Zichan was humble, respectful, kind, and fair to others.
Yan Pingzhong stayed polite to his friends even after many years.
Confucius said that thinking twice is enough before you act.
Confucius wanted peace for the old and care for the young.
Many people are as honest as me, said Confucius, but few love learning.
Yan Hui loved learning and never made the same mistake twice.
Confucius said we should help poor people, not people who are already rich.
Min Ziqian refused a job that a powerful family offered him.
Yan Hui was poor, but he was always happy.
Ziyou praised a man who never took easy roads and only visited on business.
Meng Zhifan protected the army and then said his horse was slow.
A good person needs both a good heart and good manners.
To enjoy learning is better than just to know.
Wise people like water, and kind people like mountains.
To help yourself, you must also help other people.
Confucius loved old wisdom and passed it on to others.
Confucius worried about not growing better and not teaching well.
Follow the right road, be kind, and enjoy music and art.
Confucius taught students who really wanted to learn.
Confucius would not choose a man who fights without thinking.
Plain food and water can still make a person happy.
You can learn from every person you meet on the road.
Confucius said Heaven had made him good, so he was not afraid.
Confucius fished with a line but never used a big net.
Confucius was kind, but he was also serious.
Tai Bo gave up power so quietly that no one could praise him.
Without good manners, even good qualities can become a problem.
Dying, Zengzi asked his students to look at his hands and feet.
Zengzi said that the last words of a dying man are good.
A wise person asks questions even of people who know less.
Zengzi said that the road of goodness is long.
Poems move us, good manners make us strong, and music completes us.
Study as if you can never catch up, and fear losing it.
Confucius said Yao was a great ruler who followed Heaven.
Yu ate plain food and lived simply, but worked hard for the people.
Confucius did not guess, did not insist, and did not think only of himself.
Confucius was in danger, but he trusted that Heaven would protect his teaching.
Confucius said he learned many skills only because he was poor.
Confucius said he did not know everything, and he asked many questions.
Yan Yuan said his teacher's wisdom was like a very high mountain.
Zigong asked whether he should hide a jade or sell it.
Confucius watched a river and spoke about time.
If you stop one step before the end, it is your own fault.
Only in winter do we see which trees stay green.
No one can force a person to give up his will.
In his village Confucius was quiet, but at court he spoke clearly.
At court he was friendly to junior officials and respectful to senior ones.
At the duke's gate, Confucius bent low as if it were too small.
At meals Confucius ate simple food, ate only a little, and kept quiet.
Even when the food was plain, Confucius gave thanks before eating.
A stable burned, and Confucius asked if anyone was hurt.
When a friend died with no family, Confucius said he would bury him.
When the duke called him, Confucius went at once, even on foot.
Confucius was always polite to people in mourning and to blind people.
In a carriage, he stood straight and did not look around.
Each of the students of Confucius was strong in a different way.
Going too far is as bad as not going far enough.
Confucius said that Zilu was good, but still had more to learn.
Two students asked the same question, but Confucius answered differently.
Yan Yuan came late, and Confucius was afraid he had died.
Yan Hui died, and Confucius cried with great sorrow.
Yan Hui's father asked for Confucius's carriage, but Confucius said no.
The students gave Yan Hui a grand funeral, though Confucius said no.
Zilu asked Confucius a hard question about death.
Zeng Dian wanted only a spring day by the river, and Confucius agreed.
Yan Yuan asked Confucius how to be a good person.
Do not do to others what you do not like.
A good person has no fear, because his heart is clear.
Zixia told a lonely man that good people have brothers everywhere.
A country needs food, strength, and the people's trust.
If the people have enough, the ruler will have enough too.
Each person must do his own job well.
Confucius said a leader who is not greedy will have few thieves.
When the wind blows, the grass bends over.
To be kind is to love people, and to be wise is to know them.
First, we must call things by their right names.
Confucius said an old farmer knew more about farming than he did.
Learning is not useful if you cannot use it well.
If a leader is good, people follow him without being told.
First help people have enough, then teach them.
Confucius said that in three years he could make a country good.
Confucius said that love in the family is part of doing what is right.
Good friends can think differently and still be friends.
A person is good if good people like him, not if everyone does.
A good person is calm and humble, but a proud person is never calm.
Confucius said it is shameful to care only about your pay.
Confucius said Nangong Kuo was wise because he valued goodness over strength.
It is hard to be poor and not angry, said Confucius.
In old days, people learned to improve themselves.
Qu Boyu's messenger said his master wanted to make fewer mistakes.
Confucius said that good people have no worry, doubt, or fear.
Pay kindness with kindness, and pay harm with fairness.
Confucius said that no one knew him, but Heaven did.
The gate guard said Confucius kept trying though he knew it was useless.
A passing man thought Confucius was stubborn and should stop trying.
They had no food, but Confucius stayed calm.
Confucius told Zizhang to be honest and serious, and he wrote it down.
A wise person knows when to speak and when to be quiet.
A good worker must get his tools ready first.
Be strict with yourself, be kind to others, and you will have few enemies.
People make the Way great; the Way does not make people great.
A mistake you do not fix is the real mistake.
In doing what is right, do not even give way to your teacher.
Confucius would teach anyone, whether the person was rich or poor.
Confucius led a blind musician and told him where to step.
Confucius said a ruler should worry about unfair sharing, not about being poor.
Good friends are honest and have much knowledge.
Good friends and good music help us, but too much play does not.
Speak when you are asked, and watch the face of the person you speak to.
A wise person watches himself at every age of life.
A good person respects Heaven, great people, and the words of the wise.
Some people learn easily, some need hard work, and some never try.
A good person thinks carefully about how he sees, hears, speaks, and acts.
Chase what is good, and stay away from what is bad.
Chen Gang asked if Confucius taught his own son something secret.
Yang Huo told Confucius that time passes and does not wait.
People are alike at birth but become different by habit.
Confucius joked that you do not need a big knife for a chicken.
To be good you must be respectful, generous, honest, hard-working, and kind.
Good qualities without learning can lead people into mistakes.
Poems can teach us how to live, and also the names of plants.
Good manners are more than gifts, and music is more than drums.
Heaven does not speak, yet seasons change and everything grows.
Confucius said he was sick, but then he sang so the man could hear.
Zai Wo said three years of mourning was too long, but Confucius disagreed.
Three good men tried to help a cruel king in three different ways.
A judge lost his job three times, but he did not leave home.
Duke Jing said he was too old to use Confucius, so Confucius left.
Singing girls came to Lu, and the leader forgot his work, so Confucius left.
A strange man sang to Confucius, who wanted to speak with him.
Two farmers asked why Confucius still tried to help people.
Zilu asked an old farmer about his master, but the farmer was rude.
The old man gave Zilu a good meal, but then he was gone.
Confucius said that he would not decide in advance what he must do.
Do not ask a person to be perfect, said the Duke of Zhou.
In the last books, the students speak, and they remember their teacher.
Zizhang said we should be kind to everyone, not only to good people.
Each day learn something new, and each month review what you learned.
Workers go to a workshop to make things; scholars study to find the Way.
A good person looks serious from far away but is warm up close.
Zengzi told a judge to feel pity, not joy, when he found the truth.
A good person's mistakes are seen by all, like an eclipse.
Zigong said Confucius learned something from everyone he met.
Zigong said his teacher was like the sun and moon.
Zigong said no one could ever be as great as Confucius.
Yao told Shun to hold the middle way and care for the people.
Tang prayed that he, not the people, would bear the blame.
The early Zhou rulers shared much and used fair weights and measures.
A good ruler cares about food, honesty, hard work, and fairness.
Zizhang asked how to govern, and Confucius gave him two short lists.
Help people with what they already have, and give them work they can do.
A good leader treats big and small things the same, with care.
Bad rulers punish before teaching and demand work without any warning.
When Confucius died, his students were sad for three long years.
The last book says we must listen well to know people.
B1B2: Confucius was a teacher who lived in China about 2,500 years ago. His students and their students collected his sayings in a book called the Analects.
The first book of the Analects begins with a gentle question from Confucius. He asks whether it is not a pleasure to learn something and then to practise it again and again.

The third question asks whether someone is not a true gentleman if he stays calm when others do not know his worth. Later in the same book, Confucius adds that we should worry less about being unknown and more about not knowing other people.

One of his students, Zengzi, said that he examined himself on three points every day. He asked whether he had been honest when helping others, true to his friends, and faithful to what he had been taught.
A student named You Ruo said that a person who respects his family will rarely cause trouble outside it. Goodness is like a tree, he said, and respect at home is its root.
Confucius warned that a person with clever words and a charming face is seldom truly humane. Elsewhere he says that people who are firm, simple and slow to speak are close to it.

Confucius said that young people should be respectful at home and careful and trustworthy when they go out. They should love everyone and stay close to good people, and if they have energy left, they should study.
Confucius taught that a person who is not serious will not be respected, and his learning will not be firm. If you make a mistake, he said, do not be afraid to put it right.

Zigong asked whether it was good to be poor without flattering anyone, or rich without being proud. Confucius answered that it was good, but better still to be poor and happy, or rich and fond of good manners.

To lead a large state, said Confucius, a ruler must be serious, keep his promises and spend money carefully. He must also love his people and ask them to work only at times that do not harm their farms.
In the second book, Confucius says that a ruler who leads by good character is like the Pole Star. It stays in its place, and all the other stars turn toward it.
The Book of Odes is a collection of about three hundred old poems, and Confucius loved it. He said that a single phrase in it, which means “no twisted thoughts”, sums up the whole book.

Confucius said that if rulers use only laws and punishments, people will try to avoid the punishment but will feel no shame. If rulers lead by good example, people will feel shame and correct themselves.
Looking back, Confucius said that he set his heart on learning at fifteen and stood firm at thirty. At seventy, he said, he could follow his heart's desire without ever going wrong.

Ziyou asked Confucius what it means to be a good son to one's parents. Confucius said that feeding parents is not enough, because even dogs and horses are fed, and without respect there is no difference.
Confucius said that a person who goes back over what is old and so understands what is new is fit to be a teacher. A good teacher does not only repeat the past but makes it useful today.
Confucius told his students that studying without thinking is a waste of effort. Thinking without studying, he warned, is dangerous, because a mind can wander far from the truth.
Confucius once said to his student Zilu, who was bold and eager, that he would teach him what knowledge is. When you know something, say that you know it, and when you do not, admit that you do not.
Duke Ai of Lu asked what a ruler should do to win the trust of his people. Confucius said that if he promoted honest people over crooked ones, the people would follow him.
Confucius also said that to see what is right and not to do it shows a lack of courage. Knowing the good is not enough, he believed, unless we act on it.

Book 3 begins with the Ji family of Lu, who held a dance with eight rows of dancers in their own courtyard. Only the king should have had this honour, and Confucius asked what could not be tolerated if this could be.
Confucius asked what a person without humaneness could do with ritual. He asked the same about music, because good manners and beautiful sounds are empty if the heart is not good.

A man named Lin Fang asked what the root of ritual is, and Confucius called it a great question. He answered that ceremonies should be simple rather than lavish, and that at a funeral real grief matters more than correct form.
Zixia asked Confucius about a poem that praised a woman's lovely smile. Confucius said that a painting is made after the plain white silk is ready, and Zixia replied, “Then ritual comes afterward?”

It is said that Confucius sacrificed to his ancestors as if they were present, and to the spirits as if the spirits were really there. He also said that if he did not take part himself, it was as if he had made no offering at all.

A minister named Wangsun Jia hinted that it is better to please the kitchen stove than the honoured corner of the house. Confucius answered that it is not, because a person who offends Heaven has nowhere left to pray.

When Confucius entered the Grand Temple, he asked questions about every single thing. Someone sneered that he was said to know ritual yet asked about everything, but Confucius replied that asking was the proper ritual.
Zigong wanted to stop the custom of offering a live sheep at the announcement of the new moon, which had lost its meaning. Confucius told him, “Ci, you love the sheep, but I love the ritual.”

Duke Ding of Lu asked how a ruler should treat his ministers, and how ministers should serve their ruler. Confucius answered that the ruler should treat them with ritual courtesy, and the ministers should serve with loyalty.

An official at the border town of Yi asked to meet every gentleman who passed through, and Confucius's students brought him in. Afterwards he told them not to worry about losing a position, because Heaven would use their Master as a wooden bell to wake the world.
In the fourth book, Confucius says that humaneness makes a place beautiful to live in. A person who has the choice but does not choose to live among kind people, he asks, how can he be called wise?

Confucius said that everyone wants wealth and honour, but a gentleman will not accept them if they come the wrong way. He does not leave humaneness even for the time of a single meal, not even in a hurry or in danger.
Confucius said that if a person hears the Way in the morning, he can die in the evening without regret. Few of his sayings show more clearly how much he valued finding the right path.
Confucius said that a scholar who is ashamed of poor clothes and plain food is not worth talking to. Real learning, he thought, gives a person something richer than a fine coat.
Confucius said that a person who acts only for the sake of profit will be resented by many people. Such a person always takes, and so he leaves others feeling that they have lost something.

In the fourth book, Confucius says that the gentleman understands what is right, while the small person understands only what is profitable. The question, then, is which of these two we ask first when we make a choice.

Confucius said that when we see a worthy person, we should think about how to become their equal. When we see someone who is not worthy, we should look inside ourselves and ask whether we have the same fault.

Confucius said that if parents make a mistake, a child should speak gently and stay respectful, even if they will not listen. He said that while parents are alive one should not travel far, and should always know their age, with gladness and fear.
The gentleman wants to be slow to speak but quick to act. He thought words should be chosen with care, because it is shameful when our actions fall short of them.
Confucius said that virtue is never lonely, because it always has neighbours. People who live well tend to attract others who want to live well too.

Gongye Chang had once been put in prison, but Confucius knew that he had done nothing wrong. He judged people by their character, not their troubles, and so he gave this young man his own daughter in marriage.
Zigong once asked Confucius what kind of person he was. Confucius answered that he was a vessel, and when Zigong asked which kind, he said, “A precious sacrificial vessel.”
Someone remarked that Zhonggong was a good man but not a good speaker. Confucius asked what use clever speech was, since people who always have a quick answer are often disliked.

In the fifth book, a student named Zai Wo slept through the day, and Confucius said that rotten wood cannot be carved. He added that he used to trust people's words, but now he also watches what they do.

Zigong asked why an official named Kong Wenzi was given the name Wen, which means cultured. Confucius said that he was quick, loved learning, and was never ashamed to ask questions of people below him.

Confucius praised Zichan, a wise minister of the state of Zheng, for following four of the gentleman's ways. He was modest in his conduct, respectful to his superiors, kind to the people, and fair in the work he asked of them.
Confucius said that Yan Pingzhong, an official of Qi, was very good at making friends. Even after he had known someone for a long time, he still treated that person with respect.
Ji Wenzi was an official who always thought three times before he acted. When Confucius heard this, he said that thinking twice is quite enough for a wise person.

Zilu wished to share his carriage and clothes with friends, and Yan Yuan wished never to boast of his good deeds. Asked for his own wish, Confucius hoped to comfort the old, be trusted by friends, and care for the young.
Confucius once said that in any village of ten families there must be someone as loyal and honest as he was. What that person might lack, he added, was his deep love of learning.
Duke Ai asked which of his students loved learning, and Confucius named Yan Hui. He never took out his anger on other people and never made the same mistake twice, but sadly his life was short.

Gongxi Hua went on a mission for the ruler, and Ran Qiu asked Confucius for grain for Hua's mother. Confucius suggested a small amount, but Ran Qiu gave far more, and Confucius said a gentleman helps the needy, not the rich.
The powerful Ji family wanted Min Ziqian to be an official in one of their towns. He told the messenger to refuse politely, and said that if they asked him again, he would live across the Wen River.
Yan Hui, whom Confucius admired most, lived in a narrow lane with only a bowl of rice and a cup of water. Other people would have found such a life miserable, but Yan Hui never lost his joy.

Ziyou, who ran the town of Wucheng, was asked by Confucius whether he had found any good men there. He named Tantai Mieming, who never took shortcuts and never came to Ziyou's house except on public business.

When the army of Lu was defeated, Meng Zhifan stayed behind to protect the others as they retreated. At the city gate he whipped his horse and said, “I did not dare to be last; my horse would not go forward.”
Confucius said that a person with a plain nature but no polish is like a country farmer. A person with polish but no real feeling is like a clerk, and only a balance of the two makes a gentleman.
Confucius said that knowing something is not as good as loving it. And loving it is not as good as taking real delight in it.
Confucius said that wise people delight in water and kind people delight in mountains. Wise people are active and joyful like running water, while kind people are calm, steady and long-lived.
Zigong asked whether a person who helps all the people would be called humane. He said that such a person would be a sage, and that the humane person, wanting to succeed, helps others succeed too.
Confucius said that he passed on old wisdom and did not invent new ideas. He trusted the teachings of the ancient sages and loved them, and he wanted to hand them on.
Confucius said that his worries were not improving his character and not teaching what he knew. He also worried about not doing what he knew was right, and not fixing his own faults.
Confucius gave his students a guide to life: set your heart on the Way, hold on to virtue, and rely on humaneness. After that, he added, you should enjoy the arts, such as music and archery.
Confucius said that he would only teach those who were eager to learn. If he showed a student one corner of a square and the student could not find the other three, he would stop.

Zilu, who was proud of his courage, asked whom Confucius would take if he led an army. Confucius said he would not choose someone who fought tigers bare-handed or crossed rivers without a boat, but someone careful who planned well.
Confucius said that he could eat plain rice, drink water, and sleep with his arm for a pillow, and still be happy. Wealth and honour won in the wrong way, he said, were like floating clouds to him.

Confucius said that when three people walk together, he is sure to find a teacher among them. He would copy the good qualities of one person and correct the same faults in himself when he saw them in another.
Once, a man named Huan Tui of the state of Song wished to harm Confucius. Confucius stayed calm and said that Heaven had given him his virtue, so Huan Tui could do nothing to him.
Confucius liked to fish, but he used a single line instead of a net. He also hunted with a bow, but he would not shoot at birds that were resting for the night.
The seventh book also gives us a short portrait of Confucius himself, written by his students. He was warm but strict, dignified but never harsh, and respectful and relaxed at the same time.
Confucius said that Tai Bo, an early prince of the Zhou people, had reached the highest virtue. He gave up the right to rule three times, so quietly that people could find no words to praise him.
Confucius said that respect without good manners becomes tiring, and care without good manners becomes fear. Courage without them leads to disorder, and honesty without them becomes rudeness.

When Zengzi was very ill, he called his students and asked them to look at his hands and feet. He quoted an old poem about walking on thin ice, and then said that he had kept his body safe from harm all his life.
Zengzi told his visitor that a dying bird cries sadly, but a dying man's words are good. He named three things a gentleman values: calm manners, an honest face, and speech that is never rude.

Zengzi once spoke about a friend whom he greatly admired and wished he could be like. Though able, he asked questions of people who were less able, and though he knew much, he behaved as if he knew little.
Zengzi said that a scholar must be broad-minded and strong, because his burden is heavy and his road is long. His burden is humaneness, and the road does not end until he dies.
Confucius described a path of growth that has three steps, each one linked to an art. A person is first stirred by the Odes, then made steady by ritual, and finally completed by music.
Confucius told his students to study as if they were trying to catch up with someone who was always ahead. Even after they had learned something, he said, they should be afraid of losing it.
Confucius praised the ancient king Yao as a truly great ruler. Only Heaven is great, he said, and only Yao took Heaven as his model, so the people could hardly name his goodness.
Confucius said he could find no fault in the sage-king Yu. Yu ate plain food but gave rich offerings to the spirits, and he lived in a low house but dug canals.
The students noticed that their teacher was free of four common faults. He did not make wild guesses, did not insist that he was always right, was not stubborn, and did not put himself first.

Tradition says that people of Kuang mistook Confucius for an enemy and surrounded him and his students. He said that Heaven had given him the culture of King Wen, so the men of Kuang could not stop it.

A grand minister asked Zigong how Confucius could have so many skills if he was really a sage. Confucius answered that he had been poor when young, so he had learned many humble skills, but a gentleman needs few.
Confucius said modestly that he did not possess any special knowledge. When a simple man asked him a question and he had no ready answer, he studied it from both ends until he found one.
Yan Yuan sighed that the more he looked up at his teacher's wisdom, the higher it seemed. Step by step the Master led him on, until he wanted to stop but could not.

Zigong asked whether a person with a beautiful piece of jade should hide it in a box or find a buyer. Confucius answered that it should be sold, and added that he himself was waiting for the right offer.
