Standing by a river, Confucius said that everything passes like this, never stopping by day or by night. Many readers have heard in his words a gentle reminder that time does not wait.
Confucius compared hard work to building a mountain out of earth, basket by basket. If you stop one basket short, it is your own doing, but even one more basket added is real progress.
Confucius said that only when winter comes do we see that the pine and cypress keep their leaves longest. In the same way, a person's true character shows itself most clearly in hard times.
Confucius said that a great army can lose its commander by force. But not even the strongest power can take away the will of an ordinary man.
In his home village, Confucius was modest and gentle, and he seemed almost unable to speak. In the ancestral temple and at court, however, he spoke clearly and fluently, though always with care.

At court, Confucius spoke in a relaxed and friendly way with officials of lower rank. With officials of higher rank, he spoke frankly but respectfully, and when the ruler was present, he was reverent yet at ease.
When Confucius entered the duke's gate, he bent his body forward as if the gate were too low for him. He did not stand in the middle of the doorway, and he did not step on the threshold.
Confucius did not insist on fine food, but he would not eat anything spoiled or served out of season. He never ate too much, he always had a little ginger, and he did not talk while he was eating.
Even when his meal was only coarse rice and vegetable soup, Confucius set aside a small offering before he ate. He always did this with a serious and grateful heart.
The tenth book describes how Confucius behaved in daily life, in great matters and small. When a stable burned down, he asked only whether anyone was hurt, and not about the horses.

When a friend died and had no relatives to arrange the funeral, Confucius said, “I will take care of the burial.” When friends sent him gifts, even large ones, he did not bow, unless the gift was meat from a sacrifice.
When the ruler sent for him, Confucius did not wait for his carriage to be made ready. He set off on foot at once, and his carriage followed him.

When Confucius met a person in mourning clothes, he always changed his expression, even if the person was a close friend. He also showed courtesy to officials in formal dress and to blind people, even when he knew them well.
When he rode in a carriage, Confucius stood straight and held the strap. He did not look around, he did not speak in a hurry, and he did not point at things with his hands.

Remembering the students who had stayed with him in hard times, Confucius named four kinds of talent. Among them, Yan Yuan was strong in virtue, Zigong in speech, Ran Qiu in government and Zixia in learning.

Zigong asked which was better, Zizhang or Zixia, and Confucius said that Zizhang went too far while Zixia fell short. When Zigong asked whether this meant Zizhang was better, Confucius said that going too far is as bad as not going far enough.
Some of the students looked down on Zilu because of the way he played the zither. Confucius defended him, saying that Zilu had already come up into the hall but had not yet entered the inner rooms.
Zilu asked whether he should act as soon as he heard a good idea, and Confucius told him to wait. When Ran Qiu asked the same question, Confucius told him to act at once.

After the danger at Kuang, Yan Yuan reached the group much later than the others. Confucius said, “I thought you had died,” and Yan Yuan answered, “While you are alive, Master, how would I dare to die?”
When Yan Hui died early, Confucius cried out that Heaven had destroyed him. His students said that he grieved too much, but Confucius asked, for whom, if not for this man, should he grieve?

After Yan Hui died, his father asked Confucius to sell his carriage to pay for an outer coffin. Confucius refused, saying that his own son had been buried without one, and that he could not go on foot.

When Yan Hui died, some students wanted a grand funeral for him, but Confucius said it would not be right. They held it anyway, and he said that Hui had treated him as a father, but he could not treat Hui as a son.
Zilu asked how one should serve the spirits of the dead. Confucius replied that we should first learn to serve living people, and first understand life before death.

Confucius asked his students about their wishes, and three spoke of governing states. Zeng Dian said he would bathe in the river in spring and walk home singing, and Confucius sighed, “I am with Dian.”

Yan Yuan asked Confucius what humaneness is, and the teacher said that it means mastering oneself and following good conduct. It is a matter of one's own effort, he added, and not something that depends on others.
In the same book, Confucius told his student Zhonggong not to do to others what he would not want done to himself. When he went out, he should behave as if he were meeting an honoured guest.

Sima Niu asked what makes a gentleman, and Confucius said that he is free from worry and fear. If he looks inward and finds nothing wrong, Confucius explained, what is there for him to worry about or fear?

Sima Niu sadly said that everyone else had brothers, but he had none. His fellow student Zixia comforted him, saying that a gentleman who is respectful and polite will find brothers everywhere in the world.
Zigong asked Confucius what a good government needs most in order to stand firm. He said that it needs food, weapons and trust, and that trust is the last thing it can give up.

After a bad harvest, Duke Ai complained that he did not have enough money to run his state. You Ruo advised him to tax only a tenth, because a ruler whose people have enough will never be left in need.
Duke Jing of the state of Qi asked Confucius for his advice about government. He said that everyone must truly be what he is: a ruler, a minister, a father, a son.

Ji Kangzi was troubled by the number of thieves in Lu, and he asked Confucius what to do. Confucius replied that if Ji Kangzi himself were not greedy, people would not steal, even if they were paid to do it.

A powerful minister asked whether he should punish wrongdoers to help the people follow the Way. Confucius replied that the ruler's character is the wind and the people are the grass, which bends when the wind blows.
Fan Chi asked Confucius what humaneness is, and the answer was just two short words: love people. When Fan Chi asked about wisdom, Confucius gave another short answer: know people.
Zilu asked what Confucius would do first if a ruler asked him to govern a state. He said he would put names right, because when names are wrong, words fail and nothing gets done.
Fan Chi asked to learn farming, but Confucius said an old farmer would know much more. Later he said that if a ruler loves good manners, justice and trust, people will come to him from everywhere.

What good is it, Confucius asked, to know three hundred poems if you cannot do the job you are given? If he is sent abroad and cannot answer questions on his own, then all of his learning is of little use.
Confucius said that when a ruler's own conduct is correct, things go well even without orders. When his conduct is not correct, people will not obey, even when he gives orders.
On a journey to the state of Wei, Confucius saw how many people lived there. Ran Qiu asked what should be done for them, and Confucius said that they should first be made prosperous, then taught.
Confucius once said that if a ruler would give him a position for just a year, he could make real progress. In three years, he said, he could see the work complete and the state in good order.

The Duke of She boasted that an upright man in his village had testified against his father for stealing a sheep. Confucius answered that in his own village, fathers protected their sons and sons protected their fathers, and that this was where uprightness lay.
Confucius said that the gentleman seeks harmony without demanding that everyone think alike. The small person demands that everyone agree, but cannot live in harmony.

Zigong asked if a man must be good when everyone in his village likes him, and Confucius said not necessarily. It is better, he explained, when the good people like him and the bad people dislike him.
Confucius said that a gentleman is relaxed and at ease without being arrogant. A small person, by contrast, is arrogant but is never truly at ease.
Yuan Xian asked Confucius what counts as shameful for an official. He answered that it is shameful to think only about one's salary, whether the state is well governed or not.

Nangong Kuo noted that the strong men Yi and Ao died violent deaths, while Yu and Ji, who farmed, came to rule. Confucius stayed silent, but when the man had left, he said, “What a gentleman, who values virtue so highly!”
Confucius said that it is hard to be poor without feeling resentment, but easy to be rich without being arrogant. The saying shows that he understood how much harder poverty is to bear than wealth.
Confucius said that in ancient times people studied to improve themselves. In his own day, he said, people mostly studied in order to impress other people.

Qu Boyu of Wei sent a messenger to Confucius, who asked what his master was doing these days. The man replied that his master wanted to make fewer mistakes but had not managed it yet, and Confucius admired this answer.

Confucius said that the humane are free of worry, the wise are free of doubt, and the brave are free of fear. He claimed that he had not mastered any of these, but Zigong said that his teacher was simply describing himself.

Someone once asked Confucius whether it is right to answer bad treatment with kindness. He answered that then we would have nothing to repay kindness with, so we should repay harm with fairness and kindness with kindness.

Confucius once sighed that no one understood him, and Zigong asked how that could be. He said he blamed neither Heaven nor people, since he studied what was near and reached what was high, and Heaven knew him.

Zilu spent a night at the Stone Gate, and the next morning the gatekeeper asked him where he had come from. When Zilu answered that he came from Confucius, the man said, “Is he the one who knows it is no use and keeps trying?”

In Wei, Confucius was playing a stone chime when a man with a basket stopped and said, “That player has a heart.” Then he added that the sound was stubborn, and that if no one understands you, you should simply stop.

Once, in the state of Chen, Confucius and his followers ran out of food, and the students were too weak to stand. Angry Zilu asked whether a gentleman must suffer like this, and Confucius said that a gentleman stays firm in hardship.
Zizhang asked Confucius how a person can get along well anywhere in the world. Be honest in your words and serious in your actions, said Confucius, and Zizhang wrote this on his sash.
Confucius said that if you do not speak to a person who is ready to listen, you lose that person. If you speak to someone who will not listen, you waste your words, and the wise person loses neither.
Confucius said that a craftsman who wants to do good work must first sharpen his tools. He also warns that those who ignore the distant future will soon have trouble close at hand.

Confucius said that a person who blames himself strongly and blames others lightly will keep resentment far away. Most people do the opposite, but the saying suggests that quarrels are best avoided by starting with ourselves.
Confucius said that it is people who can make the Way great, and not the Way that makes people great. A teaching does nothing on its own until someone chooses to live by it.
Confucius said that to make a mistake and not correct it is the true mistake. Everyone makes errors, but the wise person looks at his own and mends them.
Confucius said that when it comes to humaneness, a student should not give way even to his teacher. It is surprising advice from a teacher, and it shows how seriously he took goodness.
Confucius made a bold statement about education: in teaching, there should be no divisions of class. He believed that anyone willing to learn deserved to be taught, whatever family he came from.

When the blind Music Master Mian came to visit, Confucius told him where the steps and the mat were. Zizhang asked afterward whether this was how to speak to a music master, and Confucius said that it was.

When the Ji family planned to attack the small state of Zhuanyu, Confucius reproached Ran Qiu and Zilu, who served the Ji. A ruler should worry not about having too little, he said, but about sharing it unfairly.

In the sixteenth book, Confucius names three kinds of friends who help us: the upright, the trustworthy and the well-informed. He also names three kinds who harm us: those who flatter, those who please falsely, and those who talk too smoothly.

Confucius named three enjoyments that help a person: music and good manners, speaking well of others, and having many good friends. He named three that harm: showy luxury, idle wandering, and endless feasting.

Confucius named three mistakes people make when they are with a wise person. They may speak too soon, they may stay silent when they are asked, or they may speak without watching the other person's face.
Confucius said that a gentleman guards against three things at different times of life. When he is young he guards against lust, in his prime against quarrelling, and in old age against greed.

Confucius said that a gentleman holds three things in awe: the will of Heaven, great people, and the words of the sages. The small person, however, does not know the will of Heaven, and so he does not fear it.

Confucius said that people who are born knowing are the highest, and those who learn by studying come next. Next are those who learn only after meeting difficulties, and the lowest are those who struggle and still refuse to learn.

Confucius said that a gentleman has nine things to think about, from seeing clearly to speaking honestly. In doubt he asks questions, in anger he thinks of the consequences, and at the sight of profit he remembers justice.
Confucius said that when you see something good, you should chase it as if you cannot catch up. When you see something bad, you should pull back as if you had touched hot water.
Chen Gang asked Confucius's son Boyu whether his father had taught him anything special. Boyu said no, only that his father once told him to study the Odes, and another time to study the rites.
A powerful official named Yang Huo wanted Confucius to work for him, but Confucius kept away from him. When they met on the road, Yang Huo said that the years do not wait for us.
In the seventeenth book, Confucius says that people are close to one another by nature, but far apart through habit and practice. What matters most, then, is the way we choose to live each day.

At Wucheng, Confucius heard singing and music, and he joked that you do not need an ox cleaver to kill a chicken. Ziyou answered that the Master had taught that learning the Way makes a gentleman love others, and Confucius agreed that he was joking.

Zizhang asked Confucius how to be humane, and he named five things: respect, generosity, honesty, hard work and kindness. Respect protects you from insults, giving wins people over, and honesty makes others trust you.

Confucius told Zilu that six good qualities can turn into faults when they are not joined to learning. Loving kindness without learning leads to foolishness, and loving courage without learning leads to disorder.
Confucius asked his students why none of them studied the Odes. The poems, he said, can stir the heart, help us see more clearly, bring people together, and give a voice to complaint.
Confucius asked whether ritual means nothing more than offering jade and silk. He also asked whether music means nothing more than bells and drums, and his answer was clearly no.
Confucius said one day that he would like to stop speaking, and Zigong asked what the students would then pass on. Heaven does not speak, he answered, yet the seasons turn and all things grow.
Ru Bei asked to see Confucius, but Confucius sent word that he was ill. As the messenger left, Confucius took up his zither and sang loudly enough for him to hear.

Zai Wo said that three years of mourning for a parent was too long, and that one year should be enough. Confucius asked if he would feel at ease in fine clothes, and when he said yes, Confucius let him do as he pleased.
Confucius spoke of three humane men who served the last, cruel king of the Yin dynasty. Weizi left him, Jizi became his slave, and Bi Gan spoke out against him and was put to death.

Liuxia Hui, a judge in Lu, was dismissed from office three times, and people asked why he did not leave. He answered that if he served people honestly, he would be dismissed anywhere, so why leave his own land?
Duke Jing of Qi said he would honour Confucius, though not as highly as the great Ji family. Later he said that he was too old to make use of his advice, and Confucius left Qi.
The people of Qi sent a group of singing girls to Lu, and the minister Ji Huanzi accepted them. For three days he did not hold court, and Confucius, in disappointment, left the state.

A man known as the Madman of Chu passed the carriage of Confucius, singing about a phoenix whose virtue had declined. He warned that the past cannot be mended and that those who hold office now are in danger.

In the eighteenth book, two farmers told Zilu that the world could not be changed and that his teacher should withdraw from it. Confucius sighed and said that he could not live with birds and beasts, so he must stay among people.
Zilu fell behind on a journey and met an old man with a basket hanging from his staff. When asked about the Master, the old man said that a person who never farms is no master, and went on weeding.
The old man kept Zilu for the night, cooked a chicken and introduced his two sons. The next day Confucius called him a hermit, but when Zilu went back to find him, the old man had gone.
Confucius spoke of several men who had left public life in different ways, such as Bo Yi and Shu Qi. He said that he was different, because he had no fixed rule about what he must or must not do.
The Duke of Zhou gave his son, the new ruler of Lu, four pieces of advice. Do not neglect your kin, do not ignore your ministers, do not drop old friends lightly, and do not demand perfection.
The nineteenth book records the sayings of the students after their teacher's death. Zizhang says that a scholar who sees danger will give his life, and when he sees gain, he thinks of what is right.

Zixia's students told Zizhang that their teacher said to make friends with good people and turn away the rest. Zizhang answered that a gentleman respects the worthy and tolerates everyone, because if he is truly worthy, whom could he not tolerate?
Zixia said that someone who learns each day what he did not yet know shows a love of learning. If, month after month, he also does not forget what he has learned, he truly loves to learn.
Zixia compared the work of a gentleman with the work of an ordinary craftsman. Craftsmen spend their days in workshops to do their work well, he said, and gentlemen study to reach the Way.
Zixia said that others see three different sides of a true gentleman. From far away he looks stern, up close he seems warm, and when he speaks his words are firm and clear.
When the Meng family made Yang Fu a judge, he asked Zengzi for advice. Zengzi told him that rulers had lost the Way, so when he uncovered a crime, he should feel pity and not satisfaction.
Zigong said that the faults of a gentleman are like an eclipse of the sun or the moon. Everyone sees them when they happen, and everyone looks up to him again when he corrects them.
Gongsun Chao, an official, asked Zigong who had been the teacher of Confucius. Zigong answered that the Way of King Wen and King Wu lives in people, and Confucius had learned from all of them.

Later, a man told people that Zigong was wiser than Confucius, but Zigong answered that his own wall reached only the shoulder. His teacher's wall, he said, was far higher, and Confucius was like the sun and moon, which no one can climb.

Chen Ziqin told Zigong that he was being too modest, and that Confucius could not really be wiser than he was. Zigong answered that the Master could no more be equalled than the sky could be climbed by stairs.
The last book begins with the old king Yao giving his throne to Shun. He told him to follow the middle way sincerely, and warned that if the people suffer hardship, Heaven's gifts will end forever.
King Tang, who founded the Shang dynasty, offered a black bull to Heaven and prayed. He promised not to hide the good, and prayed that any guilt of the people would fall on him alone.

The early rulers of the Zhou dynasty gave generously and took the faults of the people upon themselves. They made weights and measures fair, restored old states, and raised up forgotten talents, and the people turned toward them.

The text says that what mattered most were the people, their food, the rites of mourning, and sacrifice. Generous rulers win the people, trustworthy ones are trusted, hard-working ones succeed, and fair ones make people glad.

Zizhang asked how to govern well, and Confucius answered that one must honour five excellences and banish four evils. The five are generosity without waste, work without resentment, desire without greed, dignity without pride, and awe without harshness.
Confucius explained that to be generous without waste is to help people through what they already have. To make people work without resentment, he said, is to choose tasks that they are able to do.

A gentleman never dares to be careless, said Confucius, whether he deals with many people or few, large matters or small. With neat clothes and a steady gaze, he is dignified without pride, and people look at him with awe but not fear.

Then Confucius named the four evils that a good ruler must avoid. To punish without teaching is cruel, to demand results without warning is oppressive, and to order slowly but demand speed is harmful.

Confucius died in about 479 BC, and his students mourned him for three years, as if he had been their father. The later writer Mencius says that when the others went home, Zigong stayed in a hut by the grave for three more years.
The last book ends with three things that Confucius said a person must understand: destiny, ritual and words. Without understanding words, he said, we can never really understand other people.
C1C2: Confucius, born about 551 BC in the small state of Lu, became the most famous teacher in the history of China, though in his own lifetime he held little power. He did not write the book himself, for his students and their followers collected his words over many years into twenty short books called the Analects. Reading it is like listening to conversations between a teacher and the people who came to him to learn.

The Analects opens, in its first book, with three small questions, and the first two are as gentle as a greeting. Is it not a pleasure, Confucius asks, to learn something and then put it into practice at the proper time? And is it not a joy, he adds, to have a friend arrive from a far-off place to visit you?

The third question is the hardest of the three: is a person not a true gentleman if he feels no resentment when other people fail to recognise his worth? Confucius returns to this idea later in the same book, telling his students not to be troubled that no one knows them. Their real concern, he says, should be that they do not yet know other people.

Among the voices in the first book is that of Zengzi, one of the younger students, who said that every day he examined himself on three points. Had he been loyal when planning on behalf of others, and had he been trustworthy in his dealings with friends? Last, he asked, had he actually put into practice everything that his teacher had passed on to him?

Another voice in the first book belongs to You Ruo, one of the students, who observed that a person who is respectful toward parents and elders is seldom inclined to defy those in authority. A wise person attends to the root, he said, for once the root is firm, the Way will grow. Respect within the family is the root of humaneness, the quality that Confucius valued above all.

Confucius was wary of people who spoke too smoothly, and he said so plainly in the first book. A man with clever words and an ingratiating face, he remarked, is rarely humane, because charm can be put on like a coat while goodness cannot. Elsewhere he adds that those who are firm, simple and slow to speak come close to humaneness, as though the quietest people often keep the deepest kindness.

In one short saying of the first book, Confucius sketches a whole upbringing in a single breath. A young person should be dutiful at home, respectful and trustworthy abroad, careful in speech, loving toward everyone, and close to those who are humane. Only when all of that has been done, he adds, should whatever strength remains be spent on books and culture.

Dignity and learning, the first book says, go hand in hand: a gentleman who is not serious earns no respect, and what he studies will not stand firm. He should hold loyalty and trustworthiness as his first principles, and keep company with people who share them. Above all, when he discovers a fault in himself he must not be afraid to give it up, for a mistake mended is a small thing, while a mistake defended only grows.

Zigong, always quick with a question, asked whether a man who is poor without flattering anyone and rich without being proud had reached something worthy. Confucius replied that this was good, but that it was better still to be poor and cheerful, or rich and devoted to ritual. Zigong at once quoted an ode about bone and jade being cut, filed and polished, and Confucius, delighted, said that he could now discuss the Odes with him.

Asked how a great state should be governed, Confucius gave a list that sounds almost too simple to be true. The ruler must be serious in his duties, faithful to his word, careful with the treasury, and affectionate toward his people. He must also summon them to labour only in the right season, so that the work of the court never robs the fields of their harvest.

The second book turns to government, and it begins with a picture that is easy to remember. A ruler who governs through moral character, Confucius says, is like the Pole Star, which stays in its place while all the other stars bow toward it. Real authority, the image suggests, does not push or shout; it simply draws others in by being steady and good.

The Odes, an ancient collection of about three hundred poems and songs, were Confucius's favourite reading and one of his main teaching texts. In the second book he says that a single line from them could stand for all the rest, a phrase that means having no twisted thoughts. Whatever the poet's subject, whether love, grief, war or the harvest, the aim was to feel honestly and to leave the heart straight.

Rule by orders and punishments, Confucius warned, produces people who learn only to avoid the penalty, and who feel no shame about the wrong itself. Lead them instead by example and by courtesy, and they will develop a sense of shame and, of their own accord, set themselves right. His faith was in the power of character to change a community from the inside, which no threat could ever do from the outside.

Back in the second book, Confucius gives a short summary of his own life, and it makes a fitting place to look back. At fifteen, he says, he set his heart on learning, at thirty he took his stand, and at forty he was free from doubts. At fifty he understood the will of Heaven, at sixty his ear was open to the truth, and at seventy he could follow his heart's desire without overstepping what was right.

When Ziyou asked about filial piety, Confucius answered with a sharp comparison, because the question touched something that people often forget. People nowadays, he said, think it means no more than providing for one's parents, yet dogs and horses are also fed and looked after. Unless there is genuine respect in the giving, what difference is there between the two?

Confucius held that a person who keeps the old alive by reviewing it, and who therefore comes to understand the new, is fit to be a teacher of others. The remark is a quiet warning against two opposite mistakes: the scholar who only repeats the past, and the clever man who ignores it. True teaching is a bridge, built from yesterday's wisdom and used to cross into tomorrow's problems.

Learning and thinking, Confucius taught, are two legs of the same walker, and a person who relies on only one will not travel far. A student who reads everything but never reflects ends with a head full of words and no understanding, while one who reflects without reading must build everything on his own guesses. Walking only one of these roads, he warned, leads either to wasted effort or to real danger.

In the second book Confucius turns to Zilu, a brave, impulsive student who liked to answer first and think later, and offers to teach him what knowledge really is. When you know a thing, he says, accept that you know it, and when you do not know it, accept that you do not. This honest line between what we know and what we merely suppose, he explains, is the beginning of true knowledge.

Duke Ai of Lu once asked Confucius what he must do to win the willing obedience of his people. The answer was brief and uncomfortable: raise the upright above the crooked, and the people will follow, but raise the crooked above the upright, and they will not. People watch, in other words, whom a ruler rewards, and they learn from it far more than from any speech.

To see what is right and fail to do it, the second book declares, is a lack of courage. Confucius had no patience for people who admired goodness from a safe distance, praising it in conversation and avoiding it in practice. For him, understanding and action belonged together, and a good intention that never became a deed was only half a virtue.

The third book opens with a scandal in the house of the Ji, a family of powerful ministers in Lu. They had ordered eight rows of dancers to perform in their own courtyard, a splendour that the rules of ritual reserved for the king alone. Confucius was shocked, and he asked, in effect, that if one could put up with this, then what was there that one could not put up with?

What good is ritual to a man who has no humaneness, Confucius asked, and what good is music? The question goes to the heart of his teaching, for bows, ceremonies and songs are only the outer form of something that must first exist inside a person. Without the kindness within, the most polished gesture is a mask, and the finest melody is only noise.

Lin Fang, a man of Lu, asked Confucius what lay at the root of ritual, and the Master praised the question as a great one. In ceremonies in general, he replied, it is better to be plain than extravagant, and at a funeral it is better to be truly sorrowful than to be meticulous about the form. The root, he suggests, is sincere feeling, and everything else is branches and leaves.

Zixia asked about the lines of an old poem describing a woman's lovely smile and bright eyes as a picture painted on a pure white ground. Confucius answered that the painting comes after the plain white silk, and Zixia, understanding at once, asked whether ritual might likewise come afterward. Pleased, the Master said that Zixia had lifted him up, and that now they could discuss the Odes together.

The book records that when Confucius sacrificed to his ancestors, he did so as if they were present, and when he sacrificed to the spirits, he behaved as if the spirits stood before him. He added that if he did not take part in the offering himself, it was as though no sacrifice had been made. Such rites, for him, were not a performance given by others on his behalf but an act of the heart that only he could carry out.

Wangsun Jia, a powerful official of Wei, hinted to Confucius that it is wiser to flatter the stove, which really does the work, than the honoured but idle spirit of the corner. The remark was an invitation to pay court to him rather than to the ruler. Confucius refused the bait: whoever offends Heaven, he said, has no one left to pray to.

In the Grand Temple, Confucius asked about every object and every step of the ceremony. Someone sneered that the son of the man of Zou was supposed to understand ritual, yet here he was, asking questions about everything. When the remark reached him, Confucius answered quietly that the asking was, in fact, the ritual.

At the start of each month, a sheep was offered in a ceremony that the rulers of Lu no longer even attended, and Zigong wished to do away with the sacrifice. Confucius answered him gently, using his personal name: Ci, you love the sheep, but I love the ritual. He feared that once the outward form disappeared, the last memory of the duty it stood for would vanish with it.

Duke Ding of Lu asked Confucius how a ruler ought to employ his ministers, and how ministers ought to serve the ruler. Confucius replied that the ruler should treat his ministers with courtesy and ritual, while the ministers should serve him with loyalty. The duty, in his answer, runs in both directions, so that neither side may demand from the other what it will not give itself.

A border official at Yi, who made a point of meeting every gentleman who came through, asked to see Confucius, and the students led him in. When he came out, he consoled the disciples: why should they grieve over their teacher's failure to find office, he asked, when the world had been without the Way for so long? Heaven, he said, was going to use their Master as the wooden tongue of a great bell, calling people awake.

The fourth book begins with a short sentence about a very practical matter, namely where one should make one's home. Humaneness, Confucius says, is what makes a neighbourhood beautiful, and anyone who has the freedom to choose but does not settle among the humane can hardly be called wise. It is advice about friendship as much as about housing, for the company we keep slowly shapes the person we become.

Wealth and honour are what everyone desires, Confucius admits, but a gentleman will not keep them if they cannot be gained by the proper way. Poverty and low rank are what everyone dislikes, yet he will not escape them by wrong means either. Not for the space of a single meal, he adds, does the gentleman leave humaneness, whether in haste or in danger.

If in the morning you hear the Way, Confucius says, you may die in the evening without regret. It is among the shortest sayings of the Analects and among the most striking, because it compares the value of true understanding with the value of life itself. For a man who lived by the search for the right path, one hour of real insight outweighed a lifetime of comfortable ignorance.

A scholar who has set his heart on the Way but who is ashamed of shabby clothes and coarse food, Confucius says, is not worth talking with. The judgment is harsh, but it follows from a plain principle: anyone who cares more about appearances than about the Way has not yet understood what the Way is. He himself had lived on little for long years, and he never mistook the cloth for the man.

To act with profit always in view, Confucius says, is to breed a great deal of resentment. The reason is not hard to see: where one person is always reaching for his own gain, someone else is bound to feel the loss. The saying is a small economics lesson in the cost of greed, and it is told without raising the voice.

The fourth book is full of short, sharp contrasts, and one of the best known sets two kinds of people side by side. The gentleman, Confucius says, understands what is right, while the small-minded person understands only what is profitable. The difference is not one of rank or wealth but of the question each person asks first when a choice has to be made.

Other people, in the fourth book, become a kind of mirror in which we may study our own character. When we meet someone admirable, Confucius says, we should think of how to become his equal, and when we meet someone who is not, we should turn our eyes inward and ask whether we share the fault. In this way every person we meet, good or bad, has something to teach us.

If one's parents are in the wrong, Confucius says, one should correct them gently, and if they will not listen, one should stay respectful and not complain. While they live, he adds, one should not wander far, and if one must, one should leave a fixed address. Their age, finally, is something every child ought to know, for it brings gladness at their long life and fear at how little may remain.

The same book praises a quiet kind of strength, the kind that does not need to announce itself. The gentleman, Confucius says, wishes to be slow in his speech but quick in his actions. For people of old were careful with their words, he explains, because they were ashamed to think that their deeds might fall short of them.

There is comfort in one short saying from the fourth book: virtue, Confucius says, is never alone, for it always has neighbours. A person who tries to live well may at times feel isolated, yet goodness has a way of drawing others to it, as a lit window draws travellers across a dark field. In time, those who strive for the good find that they are in good company.

The fifth book is largely a gallery of portraits, in which Confucius weighs the character of the people around him. It opens with Gongye Chang, a man who had spent time in prison, though, as the Master said, through no crime of his own. Trusting his character over his circumstances, Confucius gave him his own daughter in marriage, as a public sign of confidence.

Zigong, who was clever and rich, once asked Confucius what he thought of him. “You are a vessel,” the Master said, and when Zigong pressed him to say what sort, he answered that he was a precious sacrificial vessel, the kind used in the ancestral temple. It was praise with a gentle edge, since a gentleman, as Confucius says elsewhere, should be more than a tool for one single use.

Someone observed that Zhonggong, though perhaps humane, was not a fluent speaker, as if this were a defect worth mentioning. Confucius disagreed and asked what anyone needs eloquence for, since those who meet others with a ready tongue usually end up disliked. He added that he could not say whether Zhonggong was humane, but he was sure of one thing, which was that fluency was not the test.

The fifth book reveals that the Master, for all his gentleness, could be sharp with his students. When Zai Wo was found sleeping during the day, Confucius remarked that rotten wood cannot be carved and a crumbling wall cannot be plastered, and he asked why he should bother to scold him at all. He then added a lesson for himself: once he had trusted that people would act as they spoke, but now he listened to their words and also watched their deeds.

After his death, an official of Wei named Kong Wenzi was given the title Wen, meaning cultured, and Zigong wondered whether he truly deserved it. Confucius said that he was quick-minded and loved to learn, and that he was never ashamed to ask questions of those beneath him in rank. By that measure, the Master implies, the cultured person is not the one who knows the most, but the one who is least embarrassed to find out.

Confucius spoke warmly of Zichan, the long-serving minister of Zheng, and said that he possessed four of the qualities of a gentleman. In his own conduct he was modest, toward his superiors he was respectful, in looking after the people he was generous, and in the burdens he laid on them he was fair. The list is a small portrait of the kind of official that Confucius hoped every state might one day have.

Friendship tends to wear out not through quarrels but through familiarity, and Confucius noticed a man who avoided that fate. Yan Pingzhong, an official of Qi, was good at friendship, he said, because even after a long acquaintance he went on treating his friends with respect. It is a gentle reminder that closeness is no reason to stop being courteous.

Ji Wenzi, an official of Lu, had a reputation for caution: before he acted, he always thought the matter over three times. When this was reported to Confucius, he remarked simply that twice is quite enough for anyone. The comment is wry, and perhaps a warning that too much deliberation can become a kind of timidity, in which the right moment passes while a man is still weighing his choices.

On one occasion, as the fifth book tells it, Confucius asked two students what each most wished for. Zilu answered that he would gladly share his carriage, his horses and his fine clothes with friends, and not mind if they wore them out, while Yan Yuan hoped never to boast of his own goodness. When they turned the question back to the teacher, he said simply that he wished to give peace to the old, to be trusted by his friends, and to care tenderly for the young.

At the close of the fifth book Confucius describes himself, and he does so without boasting or false modesty. In any village of ten households, he says, there must be someone as loyal and trustworthy as he is, but there will not be anyone as fond of learning. His claim to distinction, in other words, is neither virtue nor talent but sheer appetite for study.

Duke Ai of Lu once asked Confucius which of his students truly loved to learn, and the answer came without hesitation. There was Yan Hui, he said, a man who never vented his anger on others and never repeated a mistake. But his allotted span was short, and now that he was gone, Confucius knew of no one else who loved learning in the same way, which gives the praise a note of unmistakable sorrow.

Gongxi Hua was sent on a mission to the state of Qi, and Ran Qiu asked Confucius for grain to support Hua's mother while he was away. Confucius named a modest amount, then a little more when pressed, but Ran Qiu on his own judgment handed over far more than either. Confucius reminded him that Hua already rode fat horses and wore light furs, and that a gentleman, as he understood it, helps the needy and does not make the rich richer.

The Ji family, whose power in Lu rested on questionable foundations, offered Min Ziqian a post as steward of one of their towns. He did not want to serve them, but he did not wish to insult them either, so he asked the messenger to decline politely on his behalf. If they came a second time, he said, he would be found on the far bank of the Wen River, safely out of their reach.

In the sixth book, Confucius pauses to admire Yan Hui, the student he valued above all others. How admirable he was, the teacher says, living in a narrow lane on a bamboo bowl of rice and a gourd of water, a hardship that most people could not have borne without misery. Yet through all of it, Hui's cheerfulness never changed, for his happiness did not depend on what he owned.

When Ziyou became the governor of the town of Wucheng, Confucius asked whether he had managed to find any worthy men there. Ziyou named Tantai Mieming, a man who, when he walked, never took a shortcut, and who never came to Ziyou's house except on official business. The anecdote is small, but it shows what Confucius prized in a public servant: a person whose honesty extended to the way he walked down a road.

Meng Zhifan, a man of Lu, earned the praise of Confucius for a modesty that is rare in soldiers. When his army was beaten and fell back, he stayed at the rear to cover the others. At the city gate he whipped his horse and pretended that it, not he, had been slow, so that he saved his comrades and then hid the credit behind a joke.

In the sixth book Confucius offers a recipe for good character that has just two ingredients. When a person's natural qualities outweigh his cultivation, he said, the result is rough and rustic, and when cultivation outweighs nature, the result is the showy formality of a court scribe. Only when the two are blended in equal measure, he concluded, can a man be called a gentleman.

There are three steps on the road of learning, Confucius says in the sixth book, and each is higher than the one before. To know a subject is good, but those who know are surpassed by those who love it, and those who love it are surpassed in turn by those who take delight in it. The student who has reached delight no longer feels study as a duty, because it has become one of life's pleasures.

The wise, Confucius said, take their delight in flowing water, while the humane take their delight in the mountains. The wise are always in motion, as a stream is, while the humane are still and steady, as a mountain is. The wise find happiness along the way, and the humane, in the end, are rewarded with long life.

Zigong, the eloquent student, once asked what Confucius would say of a person who could bring benefit to all the people and help everyone around him: could he be called humane? Such a person, the teacher replied, would be far more than humane, a sage, for even the legendary kings Yao and Shun would have found it hard to do so much. The humane person, he added, simply helps others to stand firm and to succeed, wishing for them what he wishes for himself.

The seventh book, which is full of the teacher's own character, opens with a modest claim: Confucius says that he passes on what he has received and does not invent, since he trusts the ancient ways and loves them. This humility is a clue to his whole mission, because he saw himself not as the inventor of a new philosophy but as the keeper of a wisdom that the sages of the past had already found. It is a rare thing for a great teacher to insist that his greatest gift is to hand something on.

Confucius, who is sometimes pictured as serene and certain, admits to worries of his own. He fears failing to cultivate his character, failing to explain what he has learned, failing to move toward what he knows is right, and failing to correct what is not good in himself. For a teacher to confess such fears is a lesson in itself, because it shows that the work of improvement never ends.

In four short clauses of the seventh book, Confucius gives a plan for a whole lifetime. Set your heart on the Way, he says, hold fast to virtue, lean on humaneness, and let your mind roam freely among the arts. The advice moves from aim to character to kindness to pleasure, as though a good life needed a purpose and a conscience but also a little play.

As a teacher, Confucius was generous with his time, but he refused to do his students' thinking for them. He would not unlock the way for a student who was not eager, he said, nor assist one who was not struggling to articulate his own thoughts. If he held up one corner of a subject and the student could not return with the other three, he would not belabour the point again.

Confucius had just praised Yan Yuan as one who could serve when called and withdraw when set aside, and Zilu, perhaps feeling overlooked, asked whom the Master would take with him to lead an army. The answer was a gentle rebuke to Zilu's own nature: he would not take a man who would fight a tiger with his bare hands or wade a river without a boat. He would choose instead someone who approached a task with caution and loved careful planning, and who saw a plan through to success.

Happiness, as the seventh book describes it, does not depend on comfort or on the opinion of others. Confucius says that there is joy to be found in eating coarse rice, drinking plain water and using a bent arm for a pillow, whereas riches and honours gained by wrong means are to him like clouds drifting past. The one is solid and lasting, the other a vapour that will soon be gone.

Among the seventh book's best-loved sayings is the observation that whenever three people are walking together, Confucius is certain to find a teacher among them. From the good qualities of one he learns what to copy, and from the faults of another he learns what to correct in himself. No one, in other words, is without something to teach, for a clear-eyed learner makes a lesson even of a stranger's mistake.

Travelling in the state of Song, Confucius learned that an officer named Huan Tui intended to do him harm. His students were afraid, but the Master was not shaken: Heaven, he said, had produced the virtue that was in him, so what could Huan Tui possibly do to him? It is the voice of a man whose confidence rests not on his own strength but on a sense of mission.

The Analects remembers a small detail of the Master's conduct that tells us much about his character. He fished with a line and a hook, never with a net that would take every fish in the stream, and when he went shooting, he would not aim at birds that were roosting. Even in his pastimes, it seems, he left the fish and the birds a fair chance.

The students who gathered these sayings sometimes stopped to describe their teacher, and the seventh book gives us a brief portrait. The Master, they say, was gentle yet stern, dignified without being fierce, and respectful while remaining perfectly at ease. It is the picture of a person who has made his character so much his own that opposite qualities sit together in him without strain.

The eighth book opens with praise for Tai Bo, an early prince of the house of Zhou, whom Confucius says had reached the highest virtue. Three times, the saying goes, he gave up the right to rule, and he did it so modestly that the people could find no way to praise him. True renunciation, it suggests, is the kind that goes almost unnoticed even by the very people who benefit from it.

Good qualities, Confucius warns in the eighth book, are not enough when they are left to stand alone. Respect without ritual becomes exhausting, caution without ritual becomes timidity, courage without ritual becomes disorder, and frankness without ritual becomes rudeness. Ritual, in this view, is the frame that gives each virtue its proper shape, so that kindness does not turn clumsy and strength does not turn into violence.

When Zengzi lay seriously ill, he called his students to his bedside and asked them to uncover his hands and feet and look at them. He then quoted a line from the Odes, about being fearful and cautious as if standing at the edge of a deep gulf or walking on thin ice. From now on, he told them, he knew that he was safe from harm, for the body that he had received from his parents had come through whole.

When the minister Meng Jingzi came to visit the ailing Zengzi, the old student greeted him with a saying: when a bird is dying, its cry is sad, and when a man is dying, his words are good. He then named three things a gentleman values: to keep violence and arrogance out of his manner, to keep his face sincere, and to keep coarse words out of his speech. A man at the end of his life, the passage suggests, sees clearly what matters most.

Zengzi once described a friend whom he had admired, and later writers have usually taken him to mean Yan Hui. Though able, this friend would ask advice of those with less ability, and though he knew much, he would ask questions of those who knew little. Though he had much, he behaved as though he had little, and when others offended him, he did not strike back.

In the eighth book, Zengzi describes what it means to take the path of learning seriously. A scholar must be broad in mind and firm in purpose, he says, for the burden is heavy and the road is long. His burden is humaneness, which is heavy indeed, and the road ends only with death, which is long indeed.

Confucius sketched the education of a person as a journey in three stages, each tied to one of the arts. First, he said, one is stirred by the Odes, when poetry awakens the feelings and teaches the heart to speak. Next one is established by ritual, which gives those feelings a steady form, and finally one is completed by music, in which the whole self is brought into harmony.

Learning, Confucius suggests in the eighth book, should be pursued with a kind of healthy anxiety. Study as though you were chasing something that you could never quite overtake, he told his students, and as though you were afraid of losing what you already had. The man who thinks that he has learned enough is already beginning to forget.

How great was Yao as a ruler, Confucius exclaimed, for only Heaven is truly great, and only Yao was able to take Heaven as his model. His kindness was so broad that the people could find no name for it, and his works shone so brightly that they became a measure for all later ages. Yao is the first of the legendary sage-kings, and the Analects turns to him whenever it wants to show what rule by virtue might look like.

Of Yu, the legendary tamer of floods, Confucius says plainly that he can find nothing to criticise. Yu ate poor food, yet he gave the spirits generous offerings, and he wore rough clothes, yet his ritual robes were splendid. He lived in a low and modest house, but he spent all his strength on ditches and canals for the good of the people.

In the ninth book, his students record that there were four failings from which the Master was entirely free. He did not rely on mere conjecture, he did not insist on certainty, he was not obstinate, and he did not make himself the centre of every question. It is a portrait of a mind that stayed open, because the one who is always sure and always right can no longer learn.

Tradition says that the people of Kuang mistook Confucius for a hated official and surrounded him and his students, and the party was in real danger. Confucius did not panic, and he reminded his followers that, with King Wen long dead, the heritage of culture now lay in his own keeping. If Heaven meant that culture to perish, a later mortal like himself could never have received it, and if Heaven did not, what could the men of Kuang possibly do?

A grand minister, curious about Confucius, asked Zigong whether the Master was a sage, since he seemed to be able to do so many things. Zigong replied that Heaven had allowed him to be a sage and had given him many abilities as well. Hearing of this, Confucius said that the minister understood him, for it was only because he had been poor in his youth that he had learned so many humble skills.

Do I possess knowledge, Confucius asks, and then he answers his own question with a firm no. He recalls a plain countryman who once put a question to him when his own mind was a blank, yet he tapped the question at both ends, as one raps a drum, until he had drawn out the whole answer. The scholar who claims to have nothing left to learn is, to Confucius, no scholar at all.

Yan Yuan, the student whom Confucius loved best, once sighed aloud with admiration for his teacher. The more he looked up at the Master's way, he said, the higher it rose, and the more he bored into it, the harder it grew. Step by step the Master drew him on, widening him with culture and restraining him with ritual, until he could not stop, and even when his strength was spent, something still towered ahead that he longed to follow.

Zigong relished a riddle, and one day he posed a question to Confucius in the form of a parable. If one possessed a beautiful piece of jade, he asked, should one lock it away in a casket, or should one seek a buyer who would pay its worth? Sell it, said Confucius, for he himself was merely waiting for a worthy offer, and he longed to put his ideas to work.

One of the most quoted moments in the ninth book is a single glance at a river. Standing beside the flowing water, Confucius said that everything passes on in just this way, never pausing, day or night. The sentence is short and says little directly, yet generations of readers have heard in it a meditation on time, on change and on the urgency of using our days well.

Confucius used the picture of a labourer building a mountain of earth to teach the value of perseverance. If the builder stops when the work is only one basket short of completion, he said, the failure is entirely his own. And if he is levelling ground and tips in even a single basket, the progress is his own as well, for the decision lies always in his own hands.

Only when the year grows cold, says Confucius, do we learn that the pine and the cypress are the last to lose their leaves. In the warm months every tree is green and every forest looks alike, so that nothing reveals which trunks are strong and which are merely fortunate. The saying has long been read as a comment on people: it is in hard times, when others fall away, that a person of steady character becomes plain to see.

In the ninth book Confucius makes a claim about the dignity of every human being. The commander of even a great army, he says, can be carried off by force, yet no power on earth can take the will of a single ordinary person. Strength, in this view, lies not in numbers or weapons but in the firmness of a purpose that no one else can seize.

The tenth book is different from the rest, for it simply describes how Confucius behaved from day to day, as seen by those who lived near him. Among his own neighbours, it says, he was modest and gentle, and he seemed almost unable to speak. In the ancestral temple and at the ruler's court, by contrast, he spoke clearly and fluently, though he always spoke with great care.

Even among officers of the court, the book notes, Confucius adjusted his manner to the person in front of him. With junior officials he spoke in a relaxed and friendly way, and with senior officials he spoke frankly but with proper respect. When the ruler himself was present, he showed reverence, yet he was never stiff, for he seemed comfortable in his dignity.

The book also notes how Confucius entered the ruler's gate, and the details show a habit of deep respect. He bent his body forward as though even the high gate were too small to let him through. He never stood in the centre of the doorway, which was the place of honour, and he took care never to step on the threshold.

The tenth book records the habits of Confucius at the dinner table with a care that is almost affectionate. He did not insist on fine rice or finely minced meat, but he refused anything that had spoiled, anything that had changed colour or smell, and anything that was out of season. He ate only modest amounts, was never without a little ginger, and did not speak while he ate.

Poor food did not excuse a careless heart, as another passage in the tenth book shows. Even when the meal was only coarse rice and a thin vegetable soup, Confucius took out a small portion and set it aside as an offering before he began to eat. He did it every time, and he did it with a serious expression, as though the plainest bowl of rice were a gift that deserved gratitude.

The tenth book is less a collection of sayings than a portrait of how Confucius behaved in his daily life, from the way he dressed to the way he spoke at court. One of its small stories tells of a morning when his stable burned down while he was away at court. Returning, he asked whether anyone had been hurt, and he did not ask about the horses, as if the answer to the first question was the only one that mattered.

The tenth book shows, in two small incidents, how Confucius treated his friends with practical loyalty. When a friend died and had no relatives to arrange the funeral, he said at once that he would take care of the burial himself. Gifts from friends, even something as valuable as a carriage and horses, he accepted without a bow, since friends hold their goods in common, though he made an exception for meat from a sacrifice.

A summons from the ruler, according to the tenth book, put Confucius in motion at once. When the duke sent for him, he did not wait for his horses to be harnessed and his carriage to be brought round. He set off on foot, and the carriage followed behind him, so that the summons was answered before the wheels had begun to turn.

Confucius, the book says, had a habit of noticing those whom life had marked. When he saw someone dressed in mourning, he changed his expression to match, even if the person was an old friend. He showed the same courtesy to officials in ceremonial caps and to blind people, whether or not he knew them well, and his good manners were never a show kept for strangers.

The tenth book turns at last to the Master in his carriage, where small habits again show a large care. He stood upright as he mounted, holding the strap, and once he was inside, he did not turn his head to look about him, did not speak in haste, and did not point with his hands. For Confucius, it seems, courtesy meant that even a rider on a public road should take care not to disturb those around him.

In the eleventh book, Confucius remembers the students who stayed with him through the hardships of his travels, and he sorts them by their gifts. For goodness of character he names Yan Yuan, Min Ziqian, Ran Boniu and Zhonggong, and for skill in speech Zai Wo and Zigong. For the business of government he names Ran Qiu and Zilu, and for learning and literature Ziyou and Zixia.

Zigong, who liked to weigh his fellow students against one another, asked Confucius which was the abler man, Zizhang or Zixia. Zizhang, the Master said, overreaches, while Zixia falls short of the mark, so that neither has quite found the balance. When Zigong concluded that Zizhang must therefore be superior, Confucius corrected him, saying that to go too far is just as much a fault as to fall short.

Confucius once complained, a little sourly, about the sound of Zilu's zither, asking what it was doing at his gate. The other students took this as permission to look down on Zilu, and the Master, seeing it, corrected them at once. Zilu had already ascended to the hall, he said, though he had not yet entered the inner rooms, meaning that he was far along in his learning but still had a way to go.

The eleventh book also shows how carefully Confucius fitted his advice to each student, for Zilu and Ran Qiu both asked whether they should act at once on what they heard. To Zilu he said wait, and to Ran Qiu he said go, and when a puzzled student asked why, he replied that one was hesitant and the other had the energy of two. A good teacher, this story shows, does not repeat the same advice to everyone but looks closely at the person who is asking.

When the party was in danger at Kuang, Yan Yuan fell behind the others and arrived long after them. The Master, who had been afraid for him, said that he had thought Yan Yuan was dead. Yan Yuan answered gently, “While you are alive, Master, how would I dare to die?”

The eleventh book also holds one of the saddest moments in the Analects, the death of Yan Hui, the student whom Confucius loved best. The old teacher cried out that Heaven had destroyed him, and he wept so bitterly that his followers told him he was grieving too much. Was that so, he asked, and for whom should he grieve, if not for such a man?

After Yan Hui's death, his father, Yan Lu, asked Confucius for his carriage so that he could sell it and buy an outer coffin for his son. Confucius refused, saying that a father speaks of his own son, whether talented or not, and that when his own son Kong Li died, he too had had a coffin without an outer one. He added that, because he ranked among those who followed the high officers, it would not be proper for him to go on foot.

When Yan Hui died, his fellow students wanted to give him a lavish funeral, but Confucius told them plainly that it would not be proper. The students nevertheless went ahead and buried him with great ceremony, against their teacher's wishes. Afterwards, with evident sorrow, the Master said that Hui had treated him as a father, but that he had not been able to treat Hui as a son, and that the fault lay with his students.

In the eleventh book Zilu, always eager for answers, asked Confucius how one ought to serve the spirits, and then asked what he thought about death. The teacher answered with two questions of his own: if a person is not yet able to serve other people, how can he serve the spirits, and if he does not yet understand life, how can he understand death? His replies turn the student back toward the work that lies in front of him, and they show how firmly the Master kept his attention on this world.

One day Confucius asked four students to say what they would do if a ruler were to recognise their talents. Zilu spoke of ruling a state, Ran Qiu of making its people prosperous, and Gongxi Hua of serving modestly at the temple, but Zeng Dian, quietly strumming his zither, laid it down and said something different. In late spring, he said, he would bathe in the Yi River with friends and boys, enjoy the breeze, and walk home singing, and Confucius sighed and said, “I am with Dian.”

The twelfth book is crowded with questions about humaneness, and the best-known of them comes from Yan Yuan, who asked what it really means. To overcome oneself and return to the ritual forms of good conduct, Confucius answered, is humaneness, and if for a single day a person could do this, everyone under heaven would turn toward humaneness. It starts with oneself, he added, and Yan Yuan answered humbly that although he was not quick, he would try to put the lesson into practice.

Zhonggong, another of the students, asked about humaneness too, and the answer he received has become one of the best-known sayings of Confucius. He told him that, on going out, he should behave as though he were receiving an honoured guest, and that he should not impose on others what he would not wish for himself. Then there would be no resentment against him, whether in the state or in his own family.

Sima Niu, one of the students, asked Confucius what it means to be a gentleman. He is free of worry and free of fear, the Master answered, and when Sima Niu wondered whether that was really all, he explained himself. If a person looks into his own heart and finds nothing to be ashamed of, he asked, what is there left to worry about or to fear?

Sima Niu once confided, with some sadness, that other people all had brothers and that he alone had none. Zixia, who had learned much from the Master, replied that life and death are fixed by fate, and that wealth and honour lie with Heaven. A gentleman who is careful in his conduct and courteous toward others, he said, will find that all people within the four seas are his brothers, so why should he grieve at having none?

Zigong asked what a government requires in order to stand, and Confucius named three things: sufficient food, sufficient weapons and the confidence of the people. If one had to be surrendered, Zigong pressed, the teacher said it should be the weapons, and if a second had to go, the food. Death comes to all, he reasoned, but a people who have lost faith in their rulers have nothing left to stand upon.

In a year of famine, Duke Ai of Lu told You Ruo that he did not have enough revenue, and he asked what could be done. You Ruo suggested taxing only a tenth of the harvest, but the duke objected that even two tenths was not enough, so how could one tenth be? If the people have enough, replied You Ruo, with whom could the ruler be left in want, and if they do not, how could he ever have plenty?

Duke Jing of the state of Qi once asked Confucius about government, and the answer is one of the shortest in the book. Let the ruler be a ruler, the teacher said, the minister a minister, the father a father and the son a son, which is to say that each person must live up to the duties of his own place. The Duke agreed warmly, saying that if the ruler failed to be a ruler and the son failed to be a son, then even with plenty of grain he could not be sure of eating it.

Ji Kangzi, the powerful minister of Lu, was troubled by thieves and asked Confucius what he should do about them. The Master's answer must have stung: if you yourself were not greedy, he said, the people would not steal, even if you rewarded them for it. The cure for a country's crime, in this view, begins in the habits of those at the top, because a people learns what to desire by watching what its rulers want.

Ji Kangzi, a powerful minister of Lu, once asked whether he should put the wicked to death in order to bring the people closer to the Way. Why use killing in government, Confucius answered, since if the minister himself desired goodness, the people would be good. The character of a gentleman is like the wind, he said, and the character of ordinary people is like the grass, and when the wind blows over the grass, the grass is sure to bend.

Fan Chi, a practical and sometimes puzzled student, asked Confucius what humaneness is, and the answer was as short as an answer can be: love people. When he asked about wisdom, the Master replied just as briefly, saying that wisdom is to know people. Fan Chi did not quite understand, so Confucius explained that if one raises the upright above the crooked, the crooked can be made straight.

In the thirteenth book Zilu asked what Confucius would do first if the Duke of Wei invited him to run the government. He would begin, the teacher answered, by putting names right, and Zilu, who thought this a long way from practical politics, protested that the Master was being unrealistic. Confucius replied that when names are wrong, speech does not make sense, and when speech does not make sense, nothing can be properly done.

Fan Chi asked Confucius to teach him farming, and the Master replied that an old farmer would know far more, and gave the same answer when asked about gardening. When Fan Chi had gone, Confucius sighed that the young man had set his sights too low. A ruler who loves ritual, justice and good faith, he said, will find that people come to him from every side with their babies on their backs, so why should he need to learn how to farm?

Learning is not meant to be an ornament, Confucius insisted, but a tool to be used in the real world. A man may recite all three hundred Odes by heart, yet if he fails when given a government post, or cannot answer for himself when sent abroad, what is his reading worth? The test of an education, in other words, is what a person can do with it when the situation is real.

Government, in the view of Confucius, is largely a matter of setting a good example. When the ruler himself is upright, he says, the people do what is right without being commanded, but when he is not upright, they will not obey even if he issues orders. Commands, then, are the least of a ruler's resources, for a people will follow what it sees long before it follows what it is told.

As Ran Qiu drove his teacher's carriage into the state of Wei, Confucius remarked on how numerous the people were. When Ran Qiu asked what should be done for such a population, the answer was to make them prosperous, and when he asked what should come after that, the answer was to teach them. The order is revealing: a hungry person cannot be expected to study virtue, but a prosperous people left without education will not remain good for long.

Confucius was never a man to boast, but in this passage he allows himself to speak of what he might do. If a ruler would only use him for a single year, he says, he could set things on a better course, and in three years the work would be accomplished. The remark has an added poignancy because few rulers ever gave him the opportunity.

The Duke of She once told Confucius, with evident pride, about an upright man in his village who had testified against his own father when the father stole a sheep. Confucius answered that the upright men of his own village were different: a father would shield his son and a son would shield his father, and uprightness lay in exactly that. The saying has been debated for centuries, because it sets the claims of family against the claims of the law, and it shows that the Analects can raise hard questions without settling them.

Harmony is not the same as agreement, according to the thirteenth book, and the difference is worth pondering. The gentleman, Confucius says, seeks harmony without insisting on sameness, while the small person insists on sameness and yet never achieves harmony. A choir, one might say, achieves its beauty through many different voices working together, not through one voice repeated.

Popularity is no proof of goodness, as the thirteenth book makes quite clear to the reader. Zigong asked whether a man could be counted as good if everyone in his village liked him, and Confucius said that this was not enough. Nor was it enough, he added, if everyone in the village disliked him, for the better test is that the good people of the village like him, and that the bad people dislike him.

The gentleman, Confucius says, is at ease without being arrogant, while the small person is arrogant without ever being at ease. It is a shrewd observation about the connection between pride and anxiety, since the person who must always prove his importance can never relax. Real dignity, the saying implies, is quiet, and it comes from knowing one's own worth without needing anyone's applause.

Yuan Xian, a student who lived a life of great simplicity, asked Confucius what counts as shameful. To think of nothing but one's salary, the Master answered, whether the state is well governed or badly governed, is a thing to be ashamed of. A public servant, in other words, owes the state more than his presence, and he should ask what he is doing for it, not only what it pays him.

Nangong Kuo, a man of Lu, put an observation about the ancient past to Confucius. The archer Yi and the strong man Ao, for all their skill and power, had met with violent ends, whereas Yu and Ji, who worked the soil with their own hands, had gone on to win the world. Confucius made no reply at the time, but once the man had left, he told his students that here was a true gentleman, one who honoured virtue above strength.

To be poor without resentment is hard, Confucius observed, and to be rich without arrogance is easy. The comparison is not a boast on behalf of the rich but a note of compassion for the poor, since it recognises how heavily hunger and want press upon a person's temper. Anyone who has watched people bear hardship gracefully will know that this is the more difficult virtue.

The fourteenth book contains a complaint about learning that will sound very familiar today. In ancient times, Confucius says, people studied for the sake of improving themselves, whereas in his own day they study in order to impress other people. The test of learning, he implies, is what it does to the learner, not how it looks to an audience.

Qu Boyu, a gentleman of Wei whom Confucius admired, once sent a messenger to visit him, and Confucius gave the man a seat and asked what his master was doing these days. My master, the messenger said, wishes to make his faults fewer, but he has not yet succeeded. When the man had gone, Confucius turned to his students and said admiringly that this was a messenger indeed, for he had spoken with both modesty and truth.

The Way of the gentleman has three parts, Confucius says in the fourteenth book, and he claims that he has not managed to practise any of them. The humane are free from worry, the wise are free from perplexity, and the brave are free from fear, yet Zigong, who had known him for many years, said gently that the Master was only describing himself. The modesty is typical, for Confucius refuses to claim even the virtues that his students see in him.

Someone once asked Confucius what he thought of repaying injury with kindness, and the teacher answered with a question of his own: with what, then, would one repay kindness? Repay injury with uprightness, he said, and repay kindness with kindness, so that each receives what it has truly earned. The saying draws a sober line between justice and generosity, for to treat the kind and the cruel in exactly the same way would be to make no difference between them at all.

In a moment of sadness that the Analects does not hide, Confucius sighed that no one understood him. Surprised, Zigong asked how that could be, and the Master answered that he blamed neither Heaven nor other people, but simply studied what lay close at hand and so reached up toward what was high. It is Heaven that knows me, he said, and the words reveal a man who, though few rulers had listened to him, still felt understood by something greater.

Zilu, travelling alone, spent the night at the Stone Gate, and in the morning the gatekeeper asked him where he had come from. He came from Confucius, Zilu replied, and the gatekeeper asked whether that was not the man who knows that it is no use and yet goes on trying. It was meant as mockery, yet it has long been read as a tribute, for it describes a man who would not give up on a world that had almost given up on him.

In the state of Wei, Confucius was striking a stone chime when a man carrying a basket passed by his door and remarked that the player must have something weighing on his heart. A moment later the stranger changed his tone and said that the clacking was stubborn and petty, and that a person whom no one understands should simply give up. Confucius answered only that the man was certainly resolute, a remark that is hard to translate and has been read in more than one way.

The fifteenth book remembers a hard time in the state of Chen, when the supplies ran out and the followers of Confucius grew so weak that none of them could rise. Zilu, his temper roused, came to the teacher and demanded to know whether even a gentleman had to suffer such hardship. Confucius replied that a gentleman certainly does, but that he holds firm in want, whereas the small person who is in want loses all restraint.

Zizhang, an ambitious student, asked Confucius how a person could make his way in the world and be understood everywhere. If your words are loyal and trustworthy and your actions serious, the Master answered, you will get along even among strangers, and if they are not, you will fail even in your own village. He told Zizhang to see these words always before him, standing or riding, and the young man wrote them on his sash.

Speech has its proper moment, Confucius teaches, and wisdom lies in knowing when that moment has come. To fail to speak with a person who is ready to be spoken with, he says, is to lose that person, while to speak with someone who is not ready is to waste one's words. The wise man, he concludes, loses neither the person nor the words, for he has learned to read the listener before he opens his mouth.

Preparation is the quiet subject of two short sayings in the fifteenth book, and both urge us to look ahead. A craftsman who wishes to do his work well, Confucius says, must first sharpen his tools, and he gave this advice to a student who had asked how to live a humane life. He adds a warning to the same effect: anyone who does not think about what lies far ahead will find sorrow waiting close at hand.

Be strict in judging yourself and lenient in judging others, Confucius said, and you will keep resentment far away. The advice sounds simple, but it asks for a reversal of what most of us do, since we are quick to explain our own failures and slow to forgive those of other people.
