A person who practises it will find that quarrels lose their fuel, because nobody can fight with someone who is already examining his own part in the trouble.

It is people who can make the Way great, Confucius said, and not the Way that makes people great. A philosophy, in other words, is only a map, and it matters nothing unless someone takes the journey. The saying places the responsibility on each person, for no teaching, however wise, will improve a life that does not choose to follow it.

A short line in the fifteenth book contains a whole philosophy of self-improvement and honesty. To have a fault and not to correct it, Confucius says, is what we should truly call a fault. Everyone goes wrong at some time, but the person who sees his error and sets it right has turned a failure into a lesson, while the one who defends his error only makes it grow.

There is a remarkable freedom in one short saying of the fifteenth book, and it is easily missed. When it comes to humaneness, Confucius tells his students, do not yield even to your teacher. A man who valued respect for elders as highly as he did nevertheless placed the claims of goodness above the claims of his own authority, which suggests that he wanted followers who would think for themselves.

Perhaps no saying of Confucius has had a longer afterlife than the claim that in teaching there are no classes. In a society where learning was largely the privilege of noble families, he took pupils of every background, from the poor Yan Hui to the wealthy Zigong, and asked of them only that they should be eager. His influence on later ages owes much to this simple refusal to divide people into those who may learn and those who may not.

When the blind Music Master Mian came to visit, Confucius guided him step by step, saying here are the steps, and then here is the mat. Once everyone was seated, he told the musician who was present in the room, naming each person in turn. After Mian had gone, Zizhang asked whether this was really the way to speak to a music master, and Confucius replied that it was exactly the way to help one.

The sixteenth book opens with a sharp conversation about a war that the Ji family was planning. The Ji intended to attack Zhuanyu, a small state nearby, and Ran Qiu and Zilu, who were serving the Ji, came to report it to their old teacher. Confucius reproached them, saying that a ruler should worry not about scarcity but about unfair sharing, and warning that the Ji's real trouble lay behind the screen wall of his own court.

The sixteenth book is built largely on lists, and one of them concerns friendship. Three kinds of friends are beneficial, Confucius says: the upright, the trustworthy, and the well-informed. Three are harmful: those who flatter, those who are ingratiating, and those who talk smoothly but have nothing to say.

Pleasures, too, can be sorted into the useful and the harmful, as Confucius shows in a pair of lists. Three kinds of enjoyment are beneficial, he says: delighting in the discipline of ritual and music, delighting in speaking of other people's good qualities, and delighting in having many worthy friends. Three kinds are harmful: delighting in showy extravagance, in idle wandering, and in feasting and revelry.

There are three errors, Confucius says, that a person can make when attending upon a gentleman. To speak before one's turn is to be hasty, and to stay silent when one is asked is to be secretive, while to speak without first observing his expression is to be blind. Good conversation, the saying suggests, is a skill of timing and attention, in which a person must know when to speak, when to hold back and how to read the one who is listening.

Each stage of life has its own temptation, Confucius says, and the gentleman is on guard against all three in turn. In youth, when the blood and energy are still unsettled, he guards against lust, and in his prime, when they are at their strongest, against the love of quarrelling. In old age, when the strength has begun to decline, the danger is greed, and a wise man holds it back as carefully as he held back the others.

Three things, Confucius says, inspire awe in the gentleman: the will of Heaven, great people, and the words of the sages. The small person, by contrast, does not know the will of Heaven and therefore does not stand in awe of it, and he treats great people with familiarity and mocks the words of the sages. The difference lies not in cleverness but in humility, for a person who respects nothing above himself has nothing to learn from.

Confucius, who denied that he had been born knowing anything, ranks people by the way in which they learn. The highest are those who know from birth, the next are those who learn by study, and after them come those who learn only after running into difficulty. The lowest of all, he says, are those who meet difficulty and still refuse to learn, which leaves almost everyone in the middle ranks, with room to improve.

Nine things, Confucius says in the sixteenth book, occupy the thoughts of a true gentleman. In seeing, he wants to see clearly, in hearing to hear sharply, in his expression to be warm, in his manner to be respectful, in speech to be loyal, and in his work to be serious. When he is in doubt he asks questions, when he is angry he considers the trouble that his anger may cause, and when he sees a chance of gain he asks himself whether it is right.

Seeing goodness, Confucius says, one should hurry toward it as if afraid of falling behind, and seeing evil, one should flinch away as if testing boiling water. He adds that he has met such people and heard such words, which is a rare note of satisfaction from a teacher who more often complained that few love virtue as they love beauty. The picture is vivid because both movements are instinctive, the first a rush forward and the second a sudden recoil.

Chen Gang suspected that Confucius might give secret teaching to his own son, and he asked Boyu whether he had heard anything unusual from his father. Boyu said that he had not, except that his father had twice asked whether he had studied the Odes and the rites, since without them he would have nothing to say and no place to stand. Chen Gang was delighted, for he had asked one question and learned three things: about the Odes, about the rites, and that a gentleman keeps a respectful distance from his own son.

Yang Huo, a powerful and unscrupulous official of Lu, wanted Confucius to serve him, and since the Master kept away, he sent him a gift of a roast piglet so that Confucius would be obliged to call. Confucius chose a time when Yang Huo was out to pay his respects, but they met on the road, where Yang Huo asked whether a man who hides his talents while his country goes astray can be called humane. The days and months pass, Yang Huo reminded him, and the years do not wait for us, and Confucius replied that he would take office.

By nature, Confucius says in the seventeenth book, people are close to one another, but through practice they grow far apart. The sentence is a quiet defence of education, for it implies that no one is born wicked or noble, and that the habits we form day after day shape the people we become. If this is so, then the most important lessons are the ones that we repeat until they become second nature.

When Confucius arrived in Wucheng, the town governed by Ziyou, he heard the sound of strings and singing in the streets. He smiled and joked that one hardly needs an ox cleaver to kill a chicken, but Ziyou answered, with some spirit, that he had once heard his teacher say that the gentleman who studies the Way loves other people. Confucius turned to his followers and said that Ziyou was right, and that his own remark had only been a joke.

Zizhang asked what it means to be humane, and Confucius answered that to practise five things anywhere in the world is to be humane. These five are respect, generosity, trustworthiness, diligence and kindness, and each, he explained, brings its own reward. The respectful are not insulted, the generous win the multitude, the trustworthy are trusted, the diligent get results, and the kind are able to lead others.

Confucius once asked Zilu whether he had heard of the six good qualities and the six blindnesses that go with them. To love humaneness without loving learning, he said, ends in foolishness, to love knowledge without learning ends in aimlessness, and to love trustworthiness without learning ends in harm. Likewise, love of straightness without learning becomes rudeness, love of courage becomes disorder, and love of firmness becomes recklessness.

Why does none of you study the Odes, Confucius asked his young followers on one occasion. The poems can stir the feelings, he said, and help a person to observe the world, to live in harmony with others, and to voice a complaint when there is cause. They teach a person how to serve his father at home and his ruler abroad, and they give him, along the way, the names of many birds, beasts, plants and trees.

People keep talking about ritual, Confucius complained, but does ritual mean no more than presents of jade and silk? They keep talking about music, he went on, but does music mean no more than bells and drums? The questions answer themselves, for gifts and instruments are only the outer shell, and what gives ritual and music their life is the respect and harmony in the hearts of those who use them.

I would rather not speak, Confucius said one day, and Zigong, alarmed, asked what his students would have to pass on if the Master said nothing. Does Heaven speak, Confucius answered, yet the four seasons run their course and the hundred things are born? The reply suggests that the deepest teaching is done by example rather than by words, in the way that nature teaches by simply being what it is.

A man named Ru Bei sent a request to see Confucius, and the Master declined on the grounds that he was ill. But as the messenger was going out of the door, Confucius took up his zither and began to sing, so that the man would hear him. The excuse was thus given and withdrawn in the same moment, and many commentators take it as a deliberate rebuke, a way of refusing without a word of argument.

Zai Wo, the student who slept in the daytime, argued that three years of mourning for a parent was far too long, since in a year the old grain is used up and the new grain ripens. Confucius asked whether he would feel at ease eating fine rice and wearing brocade after only a year, and when Zai Wo said that he would, the Master told him to do as he pleased. When Zai Wo had gone, Confucius remarked that the young man lacked humaneness, for a child is held in its parents' arms for its first three years, and three years of mourning is a small return for such care.

The eighteenth book begins with three men who answered a tyrant in three very different ways. When the last king of the Yin dynasty grew cruel, Weizi left him, Jizi became his slave, and Bi Gan spoke out plainly and was put to death. The Yin had three humane men, Confucius said, and he did not rank their choices, for each had acted out of care for the people.

Liuxia Hui, a judge in Lu who was admired for his integrity, was dismissed from office three times. Why not go and serve in another state, someone asked him, and he gave an answer that is both humorous and sad. If I serve people honestly, he said, I will be dismissed wherever I go, and if I serve them dishonestly, there is no reason to leave my homeland at all.

Confucius travelled to the state of Qi hoping that its ruler would put his ideas to use, and at first Duke Jing was warm. He could not treat him as highly as the Ji family was treated in Lu, the duke said, but he would give him a place between the Ji and the Meng. Later, however, the duke said that he was too old to use his advice, and Confucius, understanding that he would not be given a chance, left.

According to a later account, the people of Qi feared that Confucius would make Lu too strong, and so they sent a troupe of singing and dancing girls as a gift. Ji Huanzi, the powerful minister, accepted them gladly, and for three days he held no court, forgetting his duties in his pleasure. Confucius saw what this meant for the government of Lu, and he decided that he could no longer stay in the state.

Jieyu, who was known as the Madman of Chu, once walked past the carriage of Confucius, singing as he went. He addressed Confucius as a phoenix who had appeared in the wrong age, saying that the past cannot be mended, though the future can still be pursued, and that those who hold office are in danger. Confucius got down from his carriage and wished to speak with him, but the man hurried away, and Confucius could not reach him.

In the eighteenth book, two farmers ploughing a muddy field told Zilu that the world could not be changed and that his teacher would do better to withdraw from it. When Zilu reported their words, Confucius sighed and said that a person cannot live among birds and beasts, and that if he did not keep company with other people, there was no one else to keep company with. If the Way already prevailed in the world, he added, he would not be trying to change it.

Falling behind the others on a journey, Zilu met an old man who carried a basket on his staff, and he asked politely whether the man had seen his master. The old man replied that anyone who did no labour with his limbs and could not tell the five grains apart was no master of his, and then he planted his staff in the ground and began to weed. Zilu, impressed rather than offended, folded his hands respectfully and stood waiting beside the field.

The old man invited Zilu to stay the night, killed a chicken, cooked millet and introduced his two sons, and the next day Zilu told Confucius all that had happened. A hermit, the Master said, and sent Zilu back to see him, but when Zilu arrived the old man had gone out. To refuse to serve, Zilu said to the empty house, is wrong, since the duty of a gentleman is to serve even though we already know that the Way will not prevail.

In the eighteenth book, Confucius reviews the lives of several men who withdrew from the world, and he judges each one fairly. Bo Yi and Shu Qi, he says, never lowered their aims or let themselves be disgraced, while Liuxia Hui and Shao Lian bent their purposes but kept their words sound and their actions thoughtful. As for himself, he says, he is different from all of these, for he has no fixed rule about what he must do and what he must not.

The eighteenth book preserves a piece of advice that the Duke of Zhou is said to have given to his son, the first ruler of Lu. A gentleman, he said, does not neglect his own relatives, and he does not make his great ministers resent that they are not being used. He does not abandon old friends without some grave reason, and he does not demand that any one person be perfect in every way.

The nineteenth book is different from the others, for it contains no sayings of Confucius himself but the words of his students, speaking after his death. Zizhang opens it with a description of a true scholar, one who is ready to give his life in danger and who thinks of what is right when he sees a chance of gain. Such a man sacrifices with reverence and mourns with real grief, and it is, in effect, the student's way of saying what the teacher had made of him.

Some students of Zixia asked Zizhang about friendship, and he asked what their own teacher had said. Make friends with those who are good, Zixia had taught, and keep away from those who are not, but Zizhang said that he had heard something different. A gentleman, he said, honours the worthy and yet tolerates everyone, for if he is himself worthy, whom could he not tolerate, and if he is not, others will reject him in any case.

Zixia, one of the most scholarly of the students, defined the love of learning in terms of two small habits. A person who knows each day what he still lacks, he said, and who each month does not forget what he has already mastered, can truly be said to love learning. It is a modest and practical test, for it asks only for steady progress and steady review, and it measures a person by what he is adding and keeping.

Zixia offered a comparison between two kinds of work that is easy to remember and hard to forget. Craftsmen, he said, live in their workshops in order to perfect their work, and gentlemen study in order to reach the Way. In both cases the place is not an end in itself but a setting for steady practice, and the person who wants to become skilled must be willing to stay there long enough.

A gentleman presents three faces, Zixia observes, and each fits the distance from which he is seen. From far away he looks stern, and when one comes close he is found to be warm, and when he speaks, his words are firm and exact. The three impressions do not contradict one another, but combine into a single character that is dignified without coldness, kind without weakness and precise without harshness.

When Yang Fu was appointed a judge by the Meng family, he came to Zengzi for advice, and the answer he received was unexpectedly gentle. The men in authority have lost the Way, Zengzi said, and the people have long been adrift, so when you uncover the truth of a crime, feel pity rather than delight. A judge who remembers how hard the lives of ordinary people can be will, in the end, be a better judge and a kinder one.

The faults of a gentleman, Zigong said, are like an eclipse of the sun and the moon: when he makes a mistake, everyone can see it, and when he corrects it, everyone looks up to him again. The image is a consoling one, because it admits that even the best people go dark at times, and that the dark passes. What counts is not the avoidance of every error, which no one can manage, but the honesty with which it is mended.

Gongsun Chao asked Zigong where Confucius had learned all that he knew, since he seemed to have no famous teacher. The Way of Kings Wen and Wu, Zigong replied, has not fallen to the ground but still lives in people, for the worthy remember its great principles and the unworthy its smaller ones. Whom, then, could the Master not have learned from, and what single teacher would he ever have needed?

The nineteenth book gathers the sayings of the students after the Master's death, and it ends by praising him. Told that he was wiser than Confucius, Zigong answered that his own wall reached only to the shoulder, so anyone could look over it, whereas the Master's wall stood many fathoms high. Only one who finds the gate, he said, glimpses the splendour inside; others are hills that may be climbed, but Confucius is the sun and moon, which no one can surpass.

Chen Ziqin told Zigong that he was only being polite, and he asked how Confucius could really be wiser than his student. Zigong answered that one word can make a gentleman seem wise or foolish, so a person must speak carefully, and the Master could no more be matched than the sky can be climbed by stairs. Had Confucius governed a state, Zigong added, the people would have stood when he raised them and followed when he led them, and since in life he was glorious and in death mourned, how could anyone equal him?

The twentieth and last book opens with the voices of the ancient sage-kings, beginning with Yao as he hands the rule to Shun. The destiny that Heaven has appointed now rests on your person, Yao says, so hold sincerely to the Mean, for if the people fall into hardship, Heaven's bounty will end for ever. Shun, the passage adds, gave the same charge to Yu when his own time came to pass on the rule.

Tang, the founder of the Shang dynasty, is remembered in the last book for a prayer that he made when he sacrificed a black bull to Heaven. He promised that he would not pardon the guilty nor conceal the good, for the choice between them lay in the mind of Heaven. If I am guilty, he prayed, let the people not suffer for it, but if the people are guilty, let the blame rest on me.

The same passage describes the founders of the Zhou, who gave with a generous hand and who held that, if the people had faults, those faults should rest on the ruler alone. They examined weights and measures with care, reviewed the laws, and restored offices that had been abolished, and good government spread through the four quarters of the land. They revived ruined states, restored broken family lines and raised up talented men who had withdrawn from public life, and the hearts of the people turned toward them.

The passage ends with a short list of what a ruler should value: the people, their food, the rites of mourning, and the sacrifices to the ancestors. Four brief promises follow, for the generous ruler will win the crowd, and the trustworthy ruler will be trusted by the people. The diligent will succeed, and the fair will make the people glad, so that the whole art of government is gathered into four plain virtues.

The second part of the last book is a conversation in which Zizhang asks his teacher how a person should govern. Honour five excellences and banish four evils, Confucius answers, and the five are generosity without waste, labour without resentment, desire without greed, dignity without pride, and awe without harshness. Each excellence is a strength paired with its own check, so that no virtue is allowed to run to excess.

Asked to explain, Confucius said that to be generous without waste is to benefit the people through what they already have, instead of draining them to pay for gifts. To make people work without resentment is to choose the labours that they are able to do, for who would complain of that? And to desire without greed, he said, is to desire humaneness and to get it, for what greed is there in wanting to be good?

Dignity without arrogance, Confucius explained, means that the gentleman, whether he deals with many people or few, with great matters or small, never presumes to be careless. Awe without harshness comes from the way he dresses properly, composes his face and fixes his gaze, so that people who look at him feel respect and not fear. The two qualities, in other words, are the outward forms of a mind that takes everyone seriously.

Then Zizhang asked about the four evils, and Confucius replied that the first is to put people to death without having taught them, which is cruelty. The second is to demand results without giving warning, which is oppression, and the third is to give slack orders but demand a fixed deadline, which is harm. The fourth is to be stingy in handing out what has already been promised, which is the mark of a petty official, and all four describe a ruler who is hard on others and easy on himself.

Confucius died in about 479 BC, and his students, who had followed him through hardship and exile, mourned him for three years as if he had been a father. The later writer Mencius records that when the time of mourning ended, the others packed their belongings and prepared to leave, and that they bowed to one another and wept until their voices failed. Zigong, however, went back, built a hut beside the grave, and lived there alone for three more years.

The Analects closes, in its twentieth book, with a short sentence about three kinds of understanding. Without understanding destiny, Confucius says, a person cannot become a gentleman, without understanding ritual he cannot take his stand, and without understanding words he cannot know other people. For more than two thousand years, readers in China and far beyond it have returned to these plain, thoughtful sayings, finding in a teacher who claimed only to pass on old wisdom a guide for living well.
